questions.title: One Trigger Per Object: Why the Pattern Exists
questions.prompt: Why do most mature Salesforce orgs enforce a 'one trigger per object' pattern with a separate handler class, instead of just writing logic directly inside multiple triggers on the same object?
questions.modelAnswer: Salesforce does not guarantee the execution order of multiple triggers on the same object and context, so with several triggers on one object you cannot reliably predict which runs first, and a change to one trigger can silently break an assumption another trigger depends on. The one-trigger-per-object pattern fixes this by having a single, thin trigger per object and event context that simply delegates to a handler class, which then explicitly calls each piece of business logic in a defined, readable order. This also makes bulkification and testing dramatically easier, because there is one place that receives Trigger.new/Trigger.old as a whole list and one place to reason about recursion, rather than that logic being scattered and duplicated across several triggers that each have to re-implement bulk-safe patterns. It is a maintainability and predictability pattern, not a platform requirement -- multiple triggers on one object are legal and will run, just not in an order you can rely on.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it as a controllability problem more than a performance one. If I've got three triggers on Opportunity, Salesforce will run all three on insert, but it doesn't promise me an order, so six months later when someone adds a fourth trigger, I have no idea whether it'll run before or after the other three -- and if two of them touch the same field, that's a silent bug waiting to happen. With one trigger that just calls a handler class, I control the order explicitly in code, I can see the whole execution flow in one file, and bulkification only has to be done once instead of three separate times. It's really just applying normal software engineering discipline -- single entry point, explicit sequencing -- to a part of the platform that would otherwise let order become an accident.

Framing this purely as a performance optimization instead of a predictability/maintainability one

Thinking the handler pattern is a platform requirement rather than a team convention

questions.title: Bulkification: Why a SOQL Query Inside a For Loop Is a Real Bug
questions.prompt: A trigger has a for loop over Trigger.new that runs a SOQL query inside the loop to look up a related record for each Opportunity. Explain exactly why this is dangerous, not just 'inefficient,' and what governor limit it will eventually hit.
questions.modelAnswer: Apex triggers always execute against a collection of records, even when a UI action only touches one record at a time, because anything that performs a bulk operation -- a Data Loader insert, a flow updating 500 records, a Bulk API job -- fires the trigger once with all affected records in Trigger.new. A SOQL query placed inside a for loop over that collection runs once per record instead of once per transaction, so a single-record test in the UI will pass fine, but a 300-record Data Loader batch will issue 300 separate queries in one transaction. Salesforce enforces a hard limit of 100 synchronous SOQL queries per transaction (200 for asynchronous contexts), so once the batch size exceeds that threshold the transaction throws a System.LimitException: Too many SOQL queries and the entire operation rolls back -- not just the records past the limit, all of them, because Apex transactions are atomic. The fix is to move the query outside the loop, collect the needed IDs first, run one bulk query with a WHERE Id IN :idSet, and build a map for in-memory lookups inside the loop instead.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the bug that always passes code review and then blows up in production, because whoever wrote it tested with one record in the UI and it worked fine -- the problem only shows up once someone loads real volume through Data Loader or a flow that updates in bulk. What I'd actually say in the interview is: Apex doesn't know or care whether you're inserting one record or five hundred, your trigger fires once per transaction with the whole batch in Trigger.new, so if your query is inside the per-record loop, you're issuing one query per record in that same transaction. Once that batch is bigger than 100 records, you blow past the 100 synchronous SOQL limit and the whole transaction rolls back -- not a partial failure, everything. The fix is always the same shape: pull the IDs you need out of the trigger collection first, run exactly one query with an IN clause, put the results in a Map, and do lookups against that map inside the loop instead of hitting the database again.

Not knowing the synchronous SOQL limit is 100 queries per transaction (200 async)
Missing that the whole transaction rolls back atomically, not just records past the limit

questions.title: Future, Queueable, Batch, Scheduled: Picking the Right Async Tool
questions.prompt: Salesforce gives you four async Apex options -- @future methods, Queueable, Batch Apex, and Scheduled Apex. What's the real decision criteria for choosing between them, not just the textbook definitions?
questions.modelAnswer: @future methods are the simplest option for fire-and-forget work that needs to run asynchronously, usually a callout from a trigger context where synchronous callouts are disallowed, but they only accept primitive parameters (no sObjects), cannot be chained reliably, and give you no job-monitoring object. Queueable Apex supersedes @future for almost every new use case because it accepts complex types including sObjects and custom classes, supports true job chaining via System.enqueueJob inside execute(), and returns a monitorable Id you can track in AsyncApexJob. Batch Apex is the right tool specifically when you need to process a genuinely large number of records -- tens of thousands or more -- in manageable chunks, because its start/execute/finish pattern lets the platform break the full record set into batches (default scope size 200) and run each batch in its own governor-limit context, which neither future nor Queueable gives you. Scheduled Apex is not really a competing processing engine at all; it is a cron-like trigger mechanism whose job is almost always to kick off a Batch or Queueable job on a recurring schedule, not to contain heavy logic itself.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I actually decide: if it's a quick callout I need off a trigger and I don't care about chaining or monitoring, I'll still reach for Queueable over @future most of the time now, honestly, because future methods feel dated -- no sObject parameters, no real job tracking. Queueable is my default for 'this needs to happen async, might need to pass real objects, and might need a second step after it finishes.' The moment I'm talking about processing the whole Account table or a few hundred thousand records, that's Batch Apex, full stop, because the start/execute/finish shape exists specifically to chunk a huge record set and give each chunk its own fresh set of governor limits -- Queueable and future both run in a single limit context and won't survive that volume. Scheduled Apex, in my experience, is almost never where the real logic lives -- it's just the alarm clock that wakes up a batch job every night, so if someone describes complex business logic living inside a scheduled class, that's usually a sign it should've been handed off to a batch or queueable job instead.

Not knowing @future can't accept sObject parameters while Queueable can
Missing that Batch Apex's governor-limit reset per chunk is the real reason to choose it for volume
Describing Scheduled Apex as a processing engine rather than a trigger mechanism for other jobs

Queueable: accepts complex types/sObjects, true chaining, monitorable via AsyncApexJob
Batch Apex: for genuinely large record volumes, each batch gets its own governor-limit context
Scheduled Apex is a cron-like trigger for other jobs, not usually where heavy logic lives

questions.title: Synchronous vs. Asynchronous Governor Limits
questions.prompt: Name the key governor limits that differ between synchronous and asynchronous Apex contexts, and explain why async code gets more room in the first place.
questions.modelAnswer: The two limits that most commonly differ are SOQL queries per transaction -- 100 in a synchronous context versus 200 in an asynchronous one -- and CPU time, which is 10,000 milliseconds (10 seconds) synchronous versus 60,000 milliseconds (60 seconds) asynchronous. DML statement limits (150) and DML rows (50,000) stay the same across both contexts, since those scale with actual data volume rather than context type. The reason async code gets more room is that synchronous Apex is running while a user is actively waiting on a page load or a save button, so the platform caps it tightly to protect overall system responsiveness and prevent one runaway transaction from degrading everyone else's experience; asynchronous jobs run in the background with nobody staring at a spinner, so Salesforce can afford to let them run longer and do more work per transaction without the same user-facing latency pressure.
questions.professionalAnswer: The two I always bring up are SOQL queries -- 100 synchronous, 200 async -- and CPU time, 10 seconds synchronous, 60 seconds async, because those are the ones that actually bite people when they move logic between contexts. What I try to make clear is this isn't an arbitrary platform quirk: synchronous code is running in the critical path of a page load, so Salesforce deliberately keeps that window tight to protect every other user sharing that same org's resources. Async code runs detached from any one person's screen, so the platform can let it breathe more. I've actually used this directly -- when a trigger's synchronous logic was creeping toward the CPU limit because of some heavier calculation, moving that piece into a Queueable job wasn't just a style choice, it bought real headroom, six times the CPU budget, because it moved the work out of the path a user was actively waiting on.

Confusing CPU time with overall transaction time, which is a separate concern

CPU time: 10,000 ms synchronous, 60,000 ms asynchronous
DML statement (150) and DML row (50,000) limits are the same in both contexts
The gap exists because synchronous code blocks an active user session; async does not

questions.title: Lightning Data Service vs. Apex-Backed Wire Calls
questions.prompt: When should an LWC use Lightning Data Service (lightning/ui*Api wire adapters) instead of calling an Apex method with @wire or imperatively, and what do you give up by always defaulting to Apex?
questions.modelAnswer: Lightning Data Service, through adapters like getRecord, createRecord, and updateRecord from lightning/ui-record-api, gives you automatic client-side caching shared across every component on the page, built-in enforcement of field-level security and sharing without writing any server code, and offline support in mobile contexts -- and critically, because the cache is shared, if one component updates a record through LDS, every other component displaying that same record updates automatically without a manual refresh or event. The right default is LDS whenever the need is a straightforward CRUD operation on fields the UI needs to read or write directly, since it needs zero Apex code and gets FLS/sharing enforcement for free. You reach for an Apex-backed wire or imperative call when you need anything LDS can't express: a query across multiple objects, aggregate or computed values, business logic beyond a simple field read/write, or any case where the data volume or relationship complexity goes beyond what a single-record or simple list adapter supports. Defaulting to Apex for everything means losing the automatic cross-component cache synchronization and FLS enforcement LDS gives for free, and means writing and maintaining a server-side Apex class for even the simplest field display, which is unnecessary surface area.
questions.professionalAnswer: My default is LDS first, and I only drop to Apex when I hit something it genuinely can't do. If I just need to show and edit a handful of fields on a record, getRecord and lightning-record-edit-form or updateRecord do that with zero Apex, and I get something for free that people underrate -- if two unrelated components on the same page both display that record, and one of them updates it, the other one just updates too, because they're reading from the same shared LDS cache. The moment I need a cross-object query, some aggregation, or real business logic before returning data, that's not a field read anymore, that's a query, and LDS doesn't do queries -- that's when I write an Apex method and wire it in. The mistake I see junior LWC developers make is reaching for Apex by habit for everything, even a single field display, which means writing a server method, an Apex test, and losing the automatic cache sync LDS would've given them for nothing.

Missing the shared-cache cross-component sync benefit LDS provides for free
Assuming LDS can handle cross-object queries or aggregation (it can't)

questions.title: Named Credentials vs. Hardcoded Callout Endpoints
questions.prompt: Why do architects insist on Named Credentials instead of just storing an endpoint URL and an API key in a custom setting or custom metadata type for an outbound REST callout?
questions.modelAnswer: A Named Credential centralizes both the endpoint URL and the authentication (basic auth, OAuth 2.0, certificate-based, or a password/token) in one admin-managed setup object, so Apex callout code never touches or even sees the actual credential -- it just references the Named Credential by name in the callout URL, and the platform handles attaching the correct auth headers. Storing a URL and API key in a custom setting or custom metadata type means that secret value lives in a field any Apex code or report with sufficient access could potentially read, and if the credential ever needs rotating, every place that read the field directly needs to still work correctly, with no platform-level masking. Named Credentials also integrate with Salesforce's authentication provider framework for OAuth flows (handling token refresh automatically), support per-user authentication without the developer writing session-management code, and keep the actual secret out of debug logs, since callouts routed through a Named Credential don't expose the raw credential in exception or log output the way a credential sitting in a plain field might if ever mishandled.
questions.professionalAnswer: If someone proposes a custom metadata record with the endpoint and an API key sitting in a plain text field, the issue I'd raise immediately is that now that secret is just... a field, readable by any Apex code with access to that object, and potentially visible in debug logs if someone isn't careful about how it's referenced. A Named Credential moves all of that out of Apex's hands entirely -- my code just says 'callout:My_Named_Credential/endpoint' and the platform attaches the actual auth, whether that's OAuth with automatic token refresh, a cert, or basic auth, without my code ever seeing the raw secret. It also means credential rotation is an admin changing one setup record, not a deploy, and it means I never have to write or debug my own OAuth token-refresh logic, which Salesforce's auth provider framework already handles. It's one of those settings that looks like extra setup overhead the first time you configure it and then saves you from an entire category of 'how did this API key end up in a sandbox refresh or a log file' problems later.

Describing credential rotation under the custom-metadata approach as equally easy as with Named Credentials

questions.title: Change Data Capture vs. Platform Events
questions.prompt: What's the actual difference between Change Data Capture and a custom Platform Event, and when would you pick one over the other for notifying an external system of a Salesforce data change?
questions.modelAnswer: Change Data Capture (CDC) automatically publishes a change event every time a record on an enabled standard or custom object is created, updated, deleted, or undeleted, with no Apex required to fire it -- the event payload includes the changed field values plus change-type metadata, and it's subscribed to the same way as any other platform event, typically via the Streaming API or a CometD/Pub/Sub client. A custom Platform Event, by contrast, is a developer-defined event with its own custom fields and schema, which has to be explicitly published by Apex, Flow, or an external system call -- there's no automatic trigger; a developer decides exactly when and with what payload the event fires. You pick CDC when the need really is 'tell downstream systems whenever this object changes,' because it requires zero custom publish logic and guarantees you never miss a change. You pick a custom Platform Event when the business event is not a 1:1 mirror of a record's CRUD lifecycle -- for example, 'Order Approved' might involve several field changes across two objects plus some business logic, and you want one clean, purpose-built event fired at exactly the right business moment rather than subscribers having to infer that business meaning from raw field-change payloads.
questions.professionalAnswer: The distinction I'd draw is 'automatic plumbing' versus 'a business event I define.' CDC is the one where I flip a setting on an object and from then on, every insert, update, delete, or undelete on that object just publishes a change event on its own -- nobody has to remember to call anything, which is exactly why it's right for 'keep an external system's copy of this data in sync.' A custom Platform Event is the opposite -- nothing fires automatically, I have to explicitly publish it from Apex or Flow at the moment that actually matters. I reach for a custom event when the thing I care about isn't just 'a field changed,' it's a business moment -- 'this order just got approved' -- which might span multiple field changes and some validation logic, and I'd rather publish one clean, well-named event with exactly the fields a subscriber needs than make every downstream consumer reverse-engineer business meaning out of raw CDC field diffs.

questions.title: SOQL Selectivity and Why 'It Has a WHERE Clause' Isn't Enough
questions.prompt: A developer says a SOQL query is fine because it has a WHERE clause. Explain what actually makes a query selective, and why a non-selective query on a large object can still cause problems even with a filter in place.
questions.modelAnswer: Selectivity is about whether the filter in the WHERE clause can use an index to narrow the candidate set to a small percentage of the table before the query engine has to evaluate the rest of the conditions, not simply whether a WHERE clause exists syntactically. Salesforce automatically indexes a handful of standard fields (Id, Name, CreatedDate, OwnerId, and foreign-key/lookup fields) and any field explicitly marked as an External ID or flagged unique, but a filter on a non-indexed custom text or picklist field has to be evaluated by scanning, which doesn't benefit from an index at all. On a small object this doesn't matter because a full scan is cheap regardless, but once an object crosses roughly a few hundred thousand to a million rows -- genuine Large Data Volume territory -- a non-selective filter on an unindexed field can force the query optimizer to fall back to a full table scan, which risks a query timeout or, outside of a report, triggers the platform's selectivity threshold protections. The fix is either to filter on an indexed field, create a custom index (via a case with Salesforce support, or achievable yourself in some orgs) on a frequently-filtered custom field, or restructure the query to filter on a combination of fields that together push the matched row percentage below the selectivity threshold.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back gently and ask what the query's actually filtering on, because 'it has a WHERE clause' and 'it's selective' are two completely different claims. A WHERE clause on a custom picklist field with no index behind it still has to scan a huge chunk of the table to find matches -- the clause exists, it's just not helping performance at all. What actually makes something selective is filtering on a field Salesforce has indexed -- Id, standard lookup fields, CreatedDate, an External ID field, or a custom index if one's been added -- so the engine can jump straight to the matching rows instead of walking the whole object. On a small custom object with ten thousand records, none of this matters; a full scan is basically free. The moment that object is pushing into the hundreds of thousands or millions of rows, a non-selective filter is exactly the kind of thing that turns into a timeout in production that nobody saw in the sandbox, because the sandbox never had enough data to expose the problem.

questions.title: Parent-to-Child vs. Child-to-Parent Query Syntax
questions.prompt: Explain the structural difference between writing a parent-to-child subquery versus a child-to-parent dot-notation reference in SOQL, and what each one actually returns.
questions.modelAnswer: A parent-to-child query uses a nested subquery referencing the child relationship name (typically the plural relationship name, like Contacts or OpportunityLineItems) inside the outer SELECT, and returns, for each parent record, a collection of related child records accessible on that parent as a sub-list -- for example SELECT Name, (SELECT LastName FROM Contacts) FROM Account returns each Account with a nested list of its Contacts. A child-to-parent reference instead walks upward using dot notation through the relationship field, like SELECT Name, Account.Name, Account.Owner.Name FROM Contact, and returns one flat row per child record with parent and grandparent fields flattened directly onto it -- there's no nested collection, because a child has exactly one parent through a given lookup/master-detail field, so there's nothing to collect. The practical limit on the child-to-parent direction is that you can traverse up to five levels of parent relationships in a single query, while the parent-to-child direction only supports one level of child subquery nesting per relationship (though you can have multiple sibling subqueries for different child relationships in the same query).
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of it as direction matters because of cardinality -- going from parent to child, there could be many children, so the result has to be a nested list; going from child to parent, there's exactly one parent (or none), so it's just more fields flattened onto the same row, no nesting needed. If I query Account with a subquery on Contacts, each Account record in my result comes back with a little embedded list of its Contacts that I iterate separately. If I query Contact and just dot into Account.Name and even Account.Owner.Name, I get one flat row per Contact with those parent and grandparent fields sitting right on it like any other field. The syntax reflects that: parent-to-child needs the nested SELECT because it's genuinely a one-to-many shape, and child-to-parent is just dot-walking because it's many-to-one, capped at five levels up, versus the subquery side which is really one level of children per relationship, even though you can stack several different child relationships side by side in the same query.

questions.title: SOSL vs. SOQL: When Full-Text Search Actually Wins
questions.prompt: When is SOSL genuinely the better tool than SOQL, beyond 'SOSL searches multiple objects at once'?
questions.modelAnswer: SOSL's real advantage is that it performs a full-text index search across one or more fields marked as searchable, which can match on word boundaries within a text field (so searching 'Acme' can match 'Acme Corp' or 'The Acme Group') without requiring the LIKE wildcard patterns SOQL needs for partial matching, and without SOQL's selectivity concerns on an unindexed text field -- SOSL's search index is built for exactly this. It is the right tool when a user is typing a free-text search term and you genuinely don't know in advance which object (Account, Contact, Lead, Case) contains the match, since one SOSL FIND statement can return results across multiple objects in a single call, where SOQL would require a separate query per object plus a LIKE filter on each, which does not scale and will hit selectivity problems on large unindexed text fields. SOSL is the wrong tool when you already know the exact object and an indexed field to filter on (use SOQL, which supports far richer filtering, ordering, and relationship traversal), or when you need exact-match precision on structured data, since SOSL's relevance-ranked full-text matching is tuned for human search intent, not precise equality filtering.
questions.professionalAnswer: The real trigger for me is 'I don't know which object this is in, and the user just typed a word.' If someone's building a global search box and the term could be an Account name, a Contact's last name, or text inside a Case description, SOSL lets me fire one FIND statement and get ranked results back from all of those objects at once, instead of writing three or four separate SOQL queries each with a LIKE wildcard that won't use an index anyway. That unindexed-LIKE problem is actually the other half of why SOSL wins here -- a LIKE '%acme%' in SOQL on a large unindexed text field is exactly the non-selective pattern that causes timeouts at volume, while SOSL's search index is built specifically to handle that kind of free-text lookup efficiently. Where I wouldn't use SOSL is anything precise -- if I already know I'm filtering Opportunities by an exact Stage value, that's a SOQL filter on an indexed field, full stop; SOSL's relevance ranking is solving a different problem than exact structured filtering.

questions.title: Dataflows vs. Recipes in CRM Analytics
questions.prompt: CRM Analytics (formerly Tableau CRM / Einstein Analytics) offers both dataflows and recipes to prepare data for a dataset. What's the real difference, and why has Salesforce been pushing recipes as the default?
questions.modelAnswer: A dataflow is defined as raw JSON configuring a sequence of transformation nodes (digest, augment, computeExpression, and so on), authored through a visual Data Manager interface that is really editing that JSON underneath, and it runs as a single scheduled job that produces one or more output datasets. A recipe is a newer, more approachable drag-and-drop transformation builder with a visual node graph, live data preview at each step so you can see the effect of a transformation immediately rather than waiting for a full dataflow run, and a simpler mental model for common operations like joins, filters, bucketing, and formula fields. Salesforce has pushed recipes as the default because the live preview dramatically shortens the iterate-and-debug cycle compared to dataflows, where you typically have to run the whole job and inspect the resulting dataset to see if a transformation did what you expected; recipes are also easier for an analyst without deep ETL/JSON background to build and maintain, lowering the skill floor for self-service data prep, while dataflows remain available and still necessary for some advanced or legacy transformation types recipes don't yet fully cover.
questions.professionalAnswer: The dataflow is the older, more 'under the hood' option -- you're really building a chain of JSON transformation steps through a UI, and when something's wrong, you typically have to run the whole thing and then go dig through the output dataset to figure out which step produced bad data. A recipe is the same underlying idea -- clean and transform data into a dataset -- but with a visual node graph and, critically, a live preview at every step, so I can see immediately whether a join or a bucketing rule did what I expected before committing to a full run. That iteration speed is the real reason I reach for recipes first now, and it's also why Salesforce pushes them as the default entry point -- an analyst who's never touched a dataflow's JSON can build a working recipe. I'd still drop into a dataflow if I hit a transformation type recipes don't support yet, but for the large majority of day-to-day dataset prep, recipes are the faster and more maintainable choice.
commonMistakes: Describing dataflows and recipes as functionally identical with only a UI skin difference

questions.title: Shield Platform Encryption vs. Field Audit Trail
questions.prompt: An enterprise security team asks for both 'encryption at rest' and 'a full history of every field change for seven years.' Which Salesforce feature covers each requirement, and why are they not the same thing?
questions.modelAnswer: Shield Platform Encryption encrypts data at rest at the field, file, or attachment level using an org-controlled, rotatable tenant secret, so the ciphertext is what's actually written to the underlying database; it's the answer to 'protect data at rest from a storage-level breach,' but it is not a change-history feature and does not by itself extend how long field history is retained. Field Audit Trail is a separate feature that extends standard Field History Tracking's default short retention (which only keeps a limited number of field history values and a default retention window) up to ten years of retained, immutable field history, which is the correct answer for 'a complete, long-term audit trail of every tracked field change' -- often needed for regulatory compliance like FINRA's seven-year retention requirement. The two solve genuinely different problems: Shield Encryption protects data confidentiality at rest, while Field Audit Trail provides retained historical change records; an org frequently needs both together, encryption on the sensitive fields themselves and Field Audit Trail extending how long the change history on those (or other) fields survives, but implementing one does not satisfy the other requirement.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd split this into two separate asks right away, because they get confused constantly. 'Encryption at rest' is Shield Platform Encryption -- it controls what's actually sitting in the database, encrypting specific fields or files with a key the org itself controls and can rotate, so even someone with raw storage access sees ciphertext. 'Seven years of field change history' is a completely different feature, Field Audit Trail, which extends the retention of field history tracking data out to ten years instead of the much shorter default window standard field history tracking gives you. Neither one does the other's job -- turning on Shield Encryption doesn't give you longer history retention, and turning on Field Audit Trail doesn't encrypt anything. In practice, an enterprise security team asking for both usually needs both features turned on together, often encrypting the sensitive fields themselves while also extending the audit trail's retention window on those same fields, but I always walk through them as two separate configuration decisions so nobody assumes one checkbox covers both asks.

Not knowing Field Audit Trail's retention extends up to ten years
Claiming encryption at rest has any effect on field history retention length
Missing that both features are frequently needed together, not as alternatives
keyPoints: Shield Platform Encryption protects data confidentiality at rest with an org-controlled key
Field Audit Trail extends field history retention up to ten years for compliance needs
The two solve different problems and neither substitutes for the other
Enterprise compliance scenarios often need both configured together

Correctly explains what Field Audit Trail does, including retention length

questions.title: Skinny Tables and Why You Can't Just Create One Yourself
questions.prompt: What problem do skinny tables solve for a Large Data Volume org, and why is it a Salesforce-support-managed feature instead of something an admin configures directly?
questions.modelAnswer: A skinny table is a narrow, denormalized copy Salesforce maintains behind the scenes of a subset of frequently-queried fields from a large object, kept in sync with the full table automatically, so queries that only need those fields can read from the smaller, faster skinny table instead of joining across the full, wider base table and its related custom field storage structures. This matters specifically at Large Data Volume scale, where a standard query against a multi-million-row object with many custom fields has to join across the base object table and extension tables where custom fields live, and that join cost becomes a real latency problem; a skinny table collapses the needed fields into one flat structure with no join required. It is a Salesforce-support-managed feature, requested via a support case, rather than an admin-configurable setting, because skinny tables are created and maintained at the database level by Salesforce engineering, they have real constraints (a cap on the number of fields and specific field types supported, and they don't support all field types like long text areas), and getting the selection of included fields right requires understanding the org's actual query patterns, which is a deliberate architectural conversation with Salesforce, not a self-service toggle.
questions.professionalAnswer: The problem skinny tables solve is pretty specific to real LDV scale: once an object has millions of rows and a bunch of custom fields, those custom fields are actually stored in separate extension tables behind the scenes, and a normal query has to join across the base table and those extension tables to assemble the full record -- at high volume that join is expensive. A skinny table is Salesforce quietly maintaining a flat, narrow copy of just the fields you actually query most, with no join needed, kept automatically in sync with the real data. I can't just flip a setting for this myself -- it has to go through a support case, because it's genuinely a database-level object Salesforce engineering provisions and manages, there are real limits on field count and supported types, and honestly, the most important part of the request isn't the ticket itself, it's correctly identifying which fields actually belong in the skinny table based on real query patterns, because getting that wrong means you've asked for infrastructure that doesn't actually help your slow queries.

Not explaining the underlying join cost against extension tables that skinny tables avoid
Missing that skinny tables only matter at genuine multi-million-row LDV scale
Not mentioning the real constraints on field count/type that skinny tables have
keyPoints: Skinny tables are a flat, denormalized copy of select frequently-queried fields, auto-synced with the base object
They avoid the join cost against custom-field extension tables at large row-count scale
They are requested via a Salesforce support case, not self-configured by an admin
They have real constraints on field count and supported field types

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what a skinny table is and the join problem it avoids
Correctly explains why it's provisioned via support, not self-service

questions.title: Bulkifying a Trigger Handler for Field-Based Validation
questions.prompt: Write (or describe precisely) a bulk-safe trigger handler pattern for an Opportunity before-update trigger that blocks the save if Amount is reduced by more than 50% after the Opportunity reaches Stage 'Negotiation', without issuing any SOQL inside a loop.
questions.modelAnswer: The trigger itself stays a one-line delegator to a handler class, which is the standard bulk-safe pattern. The handler receives Trigger.new and Trigger.oldMap directly as the full batch -- no SOQL is needed at all here because the comparison only uses fields already present on the incoming records and their before-image via oldMap, which is free (no governor-limit cost) since it's just reading from the trigger context maps. The validation loop runs once per record in the batch regardless of batch size, and addError() on the individual record both blocks that specific record's save and surfaces a field-level error message to the user without needing a separate DML or query. This correctly handles a single-record UI save and a 200-record Data Loader batch identically, because nothing in the logic scales with batch size except the loop itself, which is O(n) and free of governor-limit risk.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd keep the trigger as a one-liner and put all the logic in the handler, because that's the pattern I want consistent across the org regardless of how simple this particular rule is. The key thing I'm making sure of here is that I'm not querying anything -- I already have both the new and old version of every record in the batch for free, through Trigger.new and Trigger.oldMap, so the percentage-drop comparison is pure in-memory math with zero governor-limit exposure no matter whether this fires for one record or a full Data Loader batch of two hundred. Using addError() on the specific Opportunity in the loop, instead of throwing an exception, means the error gets attached to that one record and shown to the user as a validation message, which is the right UX versus a generic DML exception that would roll back the whole batch with a less helpful message.
questions.example: A Data Loader batch of 200 Opportunities updating Amount will run this handler once with all 200 records in newList/oldMap -- no additional queries fire regardless of batch size.

Putting logic directly in the trigger body instead of delegating to a handler class
Throwing a generic exception instead of calling addError() on the specific record
Not null-checking Amount before dividing, which would throw a divide-by-zero or null pointer exception
keyPoints: Trigger delegates immediately to a handler class -- no logic in the trigger body
Trigger.oldMap provides the before-image for free, with no SOQL required
The loop is O(n) over the batch with no per-record governor-limit cost
addError() on the record gives per-record validation UX instead of a batch-wide exception

questions.title: Chaining Queueable Jobs for a Multi-Step Async Process
questions.prompt: Write a Queueable Apex class that processes a batch of Account records, then automatically enqueues a second job to send a summary email once the first step finishes -- demonstrating real job chaining.
questions.modelAnswer: The first Queueable's execute() method does the actual record processing in bulk -- one query, one update, both outside any loop -- and then calls System.enqueueJob to chain a second Queueable that sends the summary email, which is true job chaining: Salesforce only allows chaining one job deep from within another queueable's execute method by default (a depth-one chain limit unless increased via a specific limit increase in some editions), but that single level is exactly what's needed here. Wrapping the enqueueJob call in a Test.isRunningTest() check is a deliberate, common pattern because test context only allows one queueable job to be enqueued synchronously per test, so chaining a second job inside a test would throw a limit exception; guarding it lets the test verify the first job's logic without tripping that limit. Each job runs in its own fresh asynchronous governor-limit context, which is part of why chaining is useful here -- the email-sending step doesn't compete with the Account-processing step for the same transaction's SOQL/DML budget.
questions.professionalAnswer: The pattern here is just 'do the real work in this job, then enqueue the next step from inside execute() once the real work is done' -- that's what actual queueable chaining looks like, as opposed to just firing two unrelated async jobs independently. I query and update the accounts in bulk, no loop-bound SOQL, and only after that update succeeds do I call System.enqueueJob for the summary-email job, so the chain is sequential and dependent, not just two things happening to run async at the same time. The Test.isRunningTest() guard around the enqueue call is something I add out of habit now -- Salesforce only lets you enqueue one job synchronously inside a test context, so without that guard, any test that exercises this class and happens to also try chaining would blow past that limit and fail for a reason that has nothing to do with the actual logic being tested.

Not guarding the chained enqueueJob call with Test.isRunningTest(), causing test failures
Treating two independently-enqueued jobs as 'chaining' instead of enqueueing the second job from inside the first's execute()
Not realizing each queueable execution gets a fresh governor-limit context
keyPoints: True chaining means calling System.enqueueJob from inside execute(), not firing two separate jobs
The processing step stays bulk-safe: one query, one update, no loop-bound DML/SOQL
Test.isRunningTest() guards the chained enqueue to avoid the one-job-per-test limit
Each chained job gets its own fresh asynchronous governor-limit context

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly implements real chaining via enqueueJob inside execute()
Keeps the record-processing step bulk-safe
Correctly guards the chain for test context
Explains the fresh governor-limit context per chained job

questions.title: Writing a Batch Apex Class That Respects Scope Size
questions.prompt: Write a Batch Apex class that deactivates Contacts belonging to Accounts marked Inactive, processing in chunks of 200 (the default scope size), and explain what happens if you change the scope size in the execute call.
questions.modelAnswer: The start() method returns a QueryLocator rather than a List, which lets the batch framework query up to 50 million records (versus the much smaller row limit a List-returning start() would be capped at), and the platform automatically splits the full result set into chunks matching the requested scope size, calling execute() once per chunk with its own fresh governor-limit context -- 100 SOQL queries, 150 DML statements, 10-second CPU time, same as any synchronous-feeling chunk, available again for every single execute() call. The default scope size is 200, matching the platform's own default DML chunking size, and Database.executeBatch accepts an optional second parameter to override it; lowering the scope size (say to 50) means more total execute() invocations but less work -- and less governor-limit pressure -- per invocation, which is the right move if each record's processing is itself expensive (nested queries, callouts, complex calculations) and 200 records' worth of that work would risk hitting CPU time or heap limits within one chunk. Raising scope size above 200 is possible but increases the risk of hitting those same per-chunk limits if the per-record work is nontrivial.
questions.professionalAnswer: The main thing I want to get right here is using a QueryLocator in start(), not a List -- that's what lets this batch actually scale to the full object instead of being capped at a much smaller record count. Each execute() call gets handed exactly one chunk, sized by whatever scope size I specify, and gets its own clean set of governor limits -- so even if this ran against half a million contacts, no single execute() call is fighting for limits with any other chunk. Two hundred is the default and it's fine for something this simple, since the per-record work here is just flipping a checkbox field. If the per-record logic were heavier -- a callout per contact, say, or some expensive calculation -- I'd deliberately drop the scope size down, maybe to 50 or even 10, because fewer records per chunk means less total CPU and fewer DML rows competing for that chunk's limits, at the cost of more total chunks running. It's a real tradeoff knob, not just a performance tweak -- I size it to the actual cost of what execute() is doing per record.
commonMistakes: Using a List instead of Database.QueryLocator in start(), capping the batch's maximum processable record count
Not knowing the default scope size is 200
Assuming scope size has no real tradeoff and just picking an arbitrary large number
Forgetting each execute() chunk gets a fresh governor-limit context (assuming limits are shared/cumulative across chunks)
keyPoints: start() returning a QueryLocator scales to far more records than a List would allow
Default scope size is 200; it's an optional parameter on Database.executeBatch
Each execute() chunk gets its own fresh governor-limit context
Scope size should be tuned down when per-record processing is expensive (callouts, heavy logic)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly implements Batchable with QueryLocator in start()
Correctly states the default scope size and how to override it
Explains the fresh-governor-limit-context-per-chunk behavior
Gives a correct, concrete reason to adjust scope size

questions.title: Setting Up a Scratch Org Workflow with Salesforce DX
questions.prompt: Walk through, with actual sfdx/sf CLI commands, the steps to create a new scratch org for a feature branch, push source to it, assign a permission set, and open it in the browser.
questions.code:
# 1. Authenticate to the Dev Hub (one-time per machine, if not already authed)
sf org login web --set-default-dev-hub --alias DevHub

# 2. Create a new scratch org from the project's config, aliased for this feature
sf org create scratch --definition-file config/project-scratch-def.json \
  --alias feature-integration-fixes --duration-days 7 --set-default

# 3. Push all local source to the scratch org
sf project deploy start --source-dir force-app

# 4. Assign a permission set so the default user has the access the feature needs
sf org assign permset --name Integration_Developer

# 5. Load any sample/test data needed to exercise the feature
sf data import tree --plan data/sample-accounts-plan.json

# 6. Open the scratch org in the browser to manually verify
sf org open
questions.modelAnswer: The workflow starts with authenticating to the Dev Hub org, which is the only org capable of spawning scratch orgs and is typically authenticated once per machine rather than per feature. Creating the scratch org from a definition file (config/project-scratch-def.json) ensures every scratch org for the project gets the same baseline edition, features, and settings, rather than drifting between developers. Pushing source with the deploy command synchronizes the local force-app metadata into the brand-new, empty scratch org, since a scratch org starts with no custom metadata at all -- it's a disposable, source-driven environment by design, not a copy of production data or metadata. Assigning a permission set is a separate manual step because scratch orgs create a default admin user with System Administrator access to the org broadly, but the specific permission sets the feature's user story depends on (like Integration Developer here) still need explicit assignment to accurately reflect how a real end user's access would look when testing. Scratch orgs are source-driven and time-boxed (here, 7 days) specifically to keep developers working from version-controlled metadata rather than configuring directly in a long-lived org and risking configuration drift.
questions.professionalAnswer: The sequence I actually run looks almost exactly like this every time I start a feature: log into the Dev Hub once per machine, then for every feature branch I spin up a fresh scratch org from the shared project-scratch-def.json so it matches everyone else's baseline, not something I hand-configured. I push my local source into it immediately, because a brand-new scratch org is completely empty of custom metadata -- that's the whole point, it's disposable and rebuilt from source control every time, which is exactly what keeps 'works on my machine' configuration drift from creeping in. Assigning the permission set afterward matters because the scratch org's default user is a full admin, which is not what I want to be testing against if the actual feature depends on a more restricted permission set -- I want my manual testing to reflect what a real end user would actually see. And loading sample data before opening it in the browser means I'm not testing against an empty, meaningless org when I go to click around and verify the feature actually works.

Not using a shared scratch org definition file, causing org configuration to drift between developers
Treating a scratch org as persistent instead of disposable and time-boxed
Forgetting scratch orgs start with zero custom metadata and skipping the source push step
keyPoints: Dev Hub authentication is a one-time, per-machine setup, not per-feature
A shared scratch-org-definition file keeps every developer's scratch org baseline consistent
Scratch orgs start empty of custom metadata; source must be explicitly pushed
Permission set assignment is a separate, necessary step since the default user is a full admin

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, logically ordered sequence of sfdx/sf CLI commands
Explains why scratch orgs start empty and need source pushed
Explains why a separate permission set assignment step is needed
Notes the role of the shared scratch org definition file

questions.title: Wiring an LWC to Related Records with the Wire Adapter
questions.prompt: Write an LWC JavaScript controller that uses @wire with getRelatedListRecords (or a comparable UI API wire adapter) to display an Account's open Opportunities, reactively re-rendering if the Account record changes.
questions.modelAnswer: The @api recordId property is populated automatically by the Lightning page framework when this component is placed on an Account record page, and prefixing it with '$' in the wire configuration (parentRecordId: '$recordId') makes the wire reactive to that property -- if recordId ever changes, the wire adapter automatically re-fires and refreshes the data with zero manual refresh logic. Using getRelatedListRecords from lightning/uiRelatedListApi, rather than a custom Apex method, means this list benefits from the same Lightning Data Service caching and automatic FLS/sharing enforcement every other LDS-backed component gets -- if the user lacks access to the Opportunities related list or specific fields, the adapter handles that correctly without custom error-handling code. The where clause filters server-side rather than pulling all Opportunities and filtering in JavaScript, which keeps the payload smaller and avoids transferring data the user shouldn't necessarily be rendering client-side logic to hide. The getters (hasOpportunities, records, error) use optional chaining and nullish coalescing specifically because the wired property starts undefined before the first server response resolves, and naive property access without those guards would throw on initial render.
questions.professionalAnswer: The detail I'd call out first is the dollar-sign prefix on recordId in the wire config -- '$recordId' instead of just recordId -- because that's what makes the wire reactive; without it, the wire would only fire once with whatever recordId happened to be at component construction and never again, even if the page context changed. Using the UI API's related-list wire adapter instead of writing my own Apex method for this gets me FLS and sharing enforcement and the shared LDS cache for free, which matters because I don't want to have to re-implement access checks a platform adapter already does correctly. I always guard the getters with optional chaining, because right after the component mounts, before the server responds, that wired property is undefined, and if my getter just does this.openOpportunities.data.records without the question marks, that's a guaranteed runtime error during initial render, not an edge case -- it happens on literally every load.
questions.example: Dropping this component onto an Account record page in Lightning App Builder automatically populates recordId with the current Account's Id with no extra configuration.

Writing a custom Apex method for a simple related-list display instead of using the UI API wire adapter
Not guarding the getters against the initial undefined state before the wire resolves
Filtering records in JavaScript instead of using the adapter's server-side where clause

UI API wire adapters inherit LDS caching and automatic FLS/sharing enforcement
Server-side filtering via the where clause is more efficient than client-side filtering
Getters must guard against the wired property being undefined before the first response

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly wires getRelatedListRecords with reactive recordId binding
Correctly uses server-side filtering/sorting instead of client-side
Correctly guards against the undefined pre-resolution state
Explains the FLS/sharing enforcement benefit of the UI API adapter

questions.title: Configuring a Named Credential for an Outbound REST Callout
questions.prompt: Walk through the concrete setup steps to configure a Named Credential (and the External Credential it depends on in the newer model) for a REST callout to an external order-management system using OAuth 2.0 client credentials, then show the Apex callout that uses it.
questions.modelAnswer: In the newer (post-Winter '21-ish) Named Credential model, setup starts with creating an External Credential that defines the authentication protocol -- here, OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials -- including the token endpoint, client ID, and client secret, stored securely rather than in any field Apex can read directly. A Named Credential is then created referencing that External Credential, plus the actual callout base URL (for example https://api.ordersystem.com/v1), and a Permission Set is used to grant specific users or the running context access to that External Credential's principal, which is how per-user versus named-principal OAuth flows are controlled. In Apex, the callout endpoint is written as callout:Order_Management_API/v1/orders -- the callout: prefix tells the platform to resolve Order_Management_API through the Named Credential, attach the correct OAuth bearer token automatically (requesting and refreshing it as needed), and append the given path to the Named Credential's configured base URL. Because the credential lives entirely in setup metadata, the Apex class above contains no endpoint string, no client secret, and no manual token-refresh logic at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd set up the External Credential first, since that's where the actual OAuth mechanics live now -- client credentials flow, token endpoint, client ID and secret, all stored in setup, never in a field my Apex code can read. Then the Named Credential itself just points at the callout base URL and references that External Credential, and I use a permission set to control which users or integration context can actually use it. The payoff shows up in the Apex: all I write is callout:Order_Management_API/v1/orders as the endpoint, and the platform does the rest -- it finds the matching Named Credential, gets a valid OAuth token (requesting a new one or refreshing silently if the current one's expired), attaches it as a bearer header, and sends the request to the real URL underneath. I never see the client secret, never write refresh logic, and if that order-management system's credentials ever rotate, that's an admin updating the External Credential in setup, not a code deploy.

Not separating the External Credential (auth mechanics) from the Named Credential (endpoint + auth reference) in the newer model
Writing manual OAuth token-refresh logic that the Named Credential already handles automatically
Forgetting to grant the required permission set access to the External Credential's principal
keyPoints: External Credential defines the OAuth protocol/mechanics; Named Credential defines the endpoint plus a reference to it
Apex uses the callout: prefix and never sees the raw secret or endpoint URL directly
OAuth token acquisition and refresh are handled automatically by the platform
Permission sets control which users/contexts can use a given External Credential's principal

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the External Credential / Named Credential setup split
Correctly writes the Apex callout using the callout: prefix pattern
Explains automatic OAuth token handling by the platform
Mentions permission-set-based access control to the credential

questions.title: A Queueable That Stays Inside Governor Limits for a Large Related-Record Update
questions.prompt: Write a Queueable Apex job that updates a custom rollup field on every Account whose Opportunities changed, safely handling the case where more Accounts need updating than fit in one transaction's governor limits.
questions.modelAnswer: Rather than trying to process an unbounded list of Account IDs in a single execute() call and risking DML row or CPU limits, this job processes a fixed-size chunk (200) per execution and re-enqueues itself with whatever remains, which is the self-chaining pattern for safely working through an arbitrarily large list under Queueable's governor limits. The aggregate SOQL query (SUM with GROUP BY) computes the rollup in one query per chunk instead of looping through individual Opportunity records and summing in Apex, which is both more efficient and keeps the SOQL row count returned small regardless of how many Opportunities exist per Account. Each re-enqueued job gets its own fresh governor-limit context, so there's no cumulative limit pressure across chunks; the only real constraint is the platform's queueable job chaining depth, but because each chunk completes and starts the next from scratch, this pattern can work through a list far larger than any single transaction's limits would allow. The Test.isRunningTest() guard prevents the self-chain from firing during unit tests, since a test context only permits one synchronous queueable enqueue.
questions.professionalAnswer: The shape here is deliberately 'process a safe-sized bite, then re-enqueue myself with whatever's left' -- rather than trying to cram an arbitrarily large Account list through one execute() call and hoping it fits under the limits. I pull a fixed 200-record chunk off the front of the remaining list, compute the rollup for just that chunk using an aggregate SOQL query so I'm not looping through every Opportunity manually, update those Accounts, and if there's anything left in the list, I enqueue another instance of this same class with the remainder. Because each enqueued job gets a completely fresh set of governor limits, this pattern can chew through a list of ten thousand Account IDs just fine, five hundred at a time, without ever hitting a limit, as long as each individual chunk's work stays comfortably inside one execution's budget. The test guard is there because without it, any unit test that exercises a chunk large enough to trigger a second enqueue would fail on the one-job-per-test limit, for a reason completely unrelated to the actual rollup logic.

Not removing processed IDs from the list before re-enqueueing, causing an infinite reprocessing loop

Aggregate SOQL (SUM/GROUP BY) computes rollups in one query per chunk instead of manual summation
Each re-enqueued job gets a fresh governor-limit context
Test.isRunningTest() prevents the self-chain from breaking the one-job-per-test rule

questions.title: Writing an Optimized SOQL Relationship Query
questions.prompt: Write a single SOQL query that returns each open Opportunity along with its Account's name and billing state, and the first and last name of the Opportunity owner -- without using more than one query.
questions.code:
SELECT Id, Name, Amount, CloseDate,
       Account.Name, Account.BillingState,
       Owner.FirstName, Owner.LastName
FROM Opportunity
WHERE IsClosed = false
ORDER BY Amount DESC
LIMIT 200
questions.modelAnswer: This is a single child-to-parent query using dot notation twice -- once through the Account lookup to get Name and BillingState, and once through the Owner lookup to get FirstName and LastName -- both of which resolve in the same query execution with no additional round trips, since child-to-parent traversal just adds fields to the same returned row rather than requiring a separate query per relationship. Filtering on IsClosed, a standard boolean field, is cheap regardless of volume, and ordering by Amount with a LIMIT keeps the result set bounded, which matters both for view-state/heap considerations if this feeds a UI component and for general query performance. This correctly avoids the common mistake of running one query for Opportunities and then a second query per record (or a second bulk query) just to fetch Account or Owner fields, which would be both less efficient and, if done per-record in a loop, a governor-limit risk.
questions.professionalAnswer: The whole point here is doing it in one shot with dot notation -- Account.Name, Account.BillingState, Owner.FirstName, Owner.LastName -- rather than querying Opportunities first and then running a second query to go fetch Account or Owner details separately. Since Opportunity has exactly one Account and exactly one Owner, those are both straightforward child-to-parent traversals, and SOQL just flattens those fields right onto the same Opportunity row with zero extra round trips. I added the ORDER BY and LIMIT mostly out of habit for anything that might feed a list view or a report-like UI component, since an unbounded result set is asking for a heap or view-state problem down the line even if it wouldn't literally break today.
commonMistakes: Running a separate query to fetch Account or Owner details instead of using dot-notation traversal in one query
Omitting a LIMIT on a query that could return a large unbounded result set
Using a parent-to-child subquery where a simple child-to-parent dot reference was actually needed
Not filtering on IsClosed or an equivalent condition, returning irrelevant closed Opportunities
keyPoints: Child-to-parent dot notation resolves multiple parent relationships in a single query
No separate query is needed to fetch Account or Owner fields
A bounded result set (ORDER BY plus LIMIT) is good practice for UI-facing queries
This avoids the inefficiency of per-relationship or per-record follow-up queries

questions.title: Writing an Aggregate SOQL Query with GROUP BY and HAVING
questions.prompt: Write a SOQL query that returns each Account's total closed-won Opportunity amount for the current year, but only for Accounts where that total exceeds $100,000.
questions.code:
SELECT AccountId, SUM(Amount) totalWonAmount
FROM Opportunity
WHERE IsWon = true AND CloseDate = THIS_YEAR
GROUP BY AccountId
HAVING SUM(Amount) > 100000
ORDER BY SUM(Amount) DESC
questions.modelAnswer: GROUP BY AccountId collapses the Opportunity rows into one aggregate result per Account, with SUM(Amount) computing the total in the database rather than pulling every individual Opportunity record back to Apex and summing in a loop, which would be both less efficient and risk hitting the SOQL row-return limit on an Account with many Opportunities. The HAVING clause filters on the aggregate value itself (the computed sum) rather than a raw field, which is exactly what HAVING is for in SOQL, the same role it plays in standard SQL -- a WHERE clause could not express 'where the sum exceeds 100000' because WHERE filters individual rows before aggregation, not the aggregated result. THIS_YEAR is a SOQL date literal that correctly scopes CloseDate to the current calendar year without hardcoding specific dates that would need to be updated annually. The result is an AggregateResult collection in Apex, accessed via get('AccountId') and get('totalWonAmount') rather than standard sObject field access.
questions.professionalAnswer: I reach for GROUP BY plus SUM here specifically because I don't want to pull back every single closed-won Opportunity row and add them up myself in Apex -- that's exactly the kind of thing the database should do, and it also sidesteps any risk of hitting a row-return limit on an Account with a lot of Opportunities. The HAVING clause is the part people sometimes forget exists in SOQL -- WHERE filters individual Opportunity rows before they're grouped, but I need to filter on the summed total after grouping, and that's specifically what HAVING is for. Using THIS_YEAR instead of hardcoded dates means I'm not maintaining this query every January. The one thing to remember in Apex afterward is that this comes back as a list of AggregateResult, not Opportunity records, so I access fields with get('fieldAlias') instead of dot notation.

Pulling individual Opportunity records and summing in Apex instead of using SUM() in SOQL
Hardcoding specific calendar dates instead of using the THIS_YEAR date literal
Forgetting the result is returned as AggregateResult, not standard Opportunity sObjects

HAVING filters on the aggregated value; WHERE filters pre-aggregation rows
THIS_YEAR avoids hardcoded, manually-maintained date boundaries
Results return as AggregateResult, accessed via get(), not as sObjects

questions.title: Writing a Multi-Object SOSL Search Query
questions.prompt: Write a SOSL query that searches for the term 'Meridian' across Account names, Contact names and emails, and Case subjects, returning only a few key fields from each object.
questions.code:
FIND {Meridian} IN ALL FIELDS
RETURNING
  Account(Id, Name),
  Contact(Id, FirstName, LastName, Email WHERE LastName != null),
  Case(Id, Subject, Status WHERE Status != 'Closed')
questions.modelAnswer: FIND {Meridian} IN ALL FIELDS searches every searchable field across every object listed in RETURNING, rather than restricting the match to only name fields, which is appropriate when the search term could plausibly appear in multiple field types (an Account name, a Contact's email domain, a Case subject line). Each object in the RETURNING clause can specify its own field list and even its own WHERE clause -- here, filtering out Contacts with no last name and excluding closed Cases -- which lets a single SOSL statement return precisely scoped, per-object result sets in one call instead of three separate SOQL queries each needing their own LIKE-based filter. In Apex, this returns a List<List<sObject>>, with each inner list corresponding to one of the RETURNING object types in the order they were listed, which is a common point of confusion since it's a nested structure rather than one flat list.
questions.professionalAnswer: I used IN ALL FIELDS here instead of narrowing to IN NAME FIELDS because 'Meridian' could plausibly show up as an Account name, inside someone's email domain, or in a Case subject line, and I want all of those matched, not just name fields. The nice part about SOSL's RETURNING clause is I can attach a WHERE condition per object -- here filtering out Contacts with no last name and skipping closed Cases -- so I'm not just getting a raw unfiltered match, I'm scoping each object's results the way I actually want them. The thing I always have to remind people of in Apex afterward is that this comes back as a List of Lists, one inner list per object in the exact order I listed them in RETURNING, so results[0] is my Accounts, results[1] is Contacts, results[2] is Cases -- getting that order wrong is an easy, silent bug.
commonMistakes: Using IN NAME FIELDS when the search term could plausibly match non-name fields like email or subject
Not using per-object WHERE clauses available inside RETURNING to scope results further
Forgetting the Apex return type is a nested List<List<sObject>>, not a flat list
Mismatching the expected inner-list order against the order objects were listed in RETURNING

RETURNING supports a separate field list and WHERE clause per object
A single SOSL call replaces several separate per-object SOQL queries with LIKE filters
Apex receives a List<List<sObject>>, ordered to match the RETURNING clause's object order

questions.title: Configuring a CRM Analytics Recipe Transformation
questions.prompt: Walk through the concrete steps to build a CRM Analytics recipe that joins Opportunity data to Account data, buckets Amount into pipeline-size tiers, and outputs a dataset ready for a dashboard -- as if you were actually clicking through the recipe builder.
questions.modelAnswer: First, add the Opportunity object as the recipe's primary input node, then add Account as a second input node and connect a Join transformation node between them, joining on AccountId to Account.Id with a left join so Opportunities without a matching Account (if any exist due to data quality issues) aren't silently dropped. Next, add a Transform node with a Bucket (formula or bucketing UI) transformation on the joined Amount field, defining tiers such as 'Small' (under 10,000), 'Mid' (10,000-99,999), and 'Large' (100,000 and above) as a new text column. After the bucket transformation, add a Select/Output node to choose which final columns feed the output dataset -- keeping only the fields the dashboard actually needs, like Opportunity Name, Amount, the new Pipeline_Tier bucket, Account Name, and Account Industry -- rather than carrying every input field forward into the dataset. Finally, configure the output dataset's name and the recipe's run schedule (or trigger it manually to test), and use the recipe's live preview at each node along the way to confirm the join and bucket logic produced the expected result before committing to a scheduled run.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build this left to right, checking the live preview at every node rather than wiring the whole thing blind and hoping it's right at the end. Opportunity goes in as the base input, I add Account as a second input, then a join node connecting AccountId to the Account's Id -- and I'd use a left join specifically, because if there's ever an Opportunity with a null or orphaned AccountId, I don't want that row to just vanish from the dataset without me knowing about it. Once joined, I add the bucket transformation on Amount, defining my tiers right there in the UI, and I'll check the preview immediately to make sure, say, a $95,000 deal actually lands in 'Mid' and not accidentally in 'Large.' Before the output node, I trim the columns down to just what the dashboard actually needs -- there's no reason to carry every single Account and Opportunity field into the final dataset just because they were available upstream. Then I name the output dataset clearly and either schedule it or run it manually the first few times until I trust it, using the live preview the whole way through instead of only checking the result after a full run.

Not checking the live preview at each step, discovering a bad bucket boundary only after a full run
Carrying every input field into the final output dataset instead of trimming to what's actually needed
Hardcoding bucket boundaries without confirming them against actual sample data in the preview

questions.prompt: Write a dbt staging model (SQL) that cleans a raw Salesforce Opportunity extract table -- standardizing the stage name casing, filtering out test/dummy records, and casting Amount to a consistent numeric type.

-- models/staging/stg_salesforce__opportunities.sql

with source as (
    select * from {{ source('salesforce', 'opportunity_raw') }}
),

cleaned as (
    select
        id as opportunity_id,
        account_id,
        trim(initcap(stage_name)) as stage_name,
        cast(amount as numeric(18,2)) as amount,

        is_won,
        is_closed,
        created_date

questions.modelAnswer: This is a standard two-CTE staging model: the source CTE pulls from the raw table via the source() macro, which keeps the lineage explicit and lets dbt track dependencies and freshness against the actual raw source definition, rather than hardcoding a schema.table reference directly in the model. The cleaned CTE does exactly the three things a staging model should do and nothing more -- light standardization (trim/initcap on stage_name to fix inconsistent casing coming from manual data entry or multiple integration sources), type casting (Amount to a fixed-precision numeric rather than trusting whatever loose type the raw extract landed as), and filtering out records that shouldn't enter the analytics layer at all (test/dummy Opportunities and ones with a null AccountId, which would break downstream joins). questions.title: Debugging 'Too Many SOQL Queries: 101'
questions.prompt: A nightly batch job that updates Contacts starts throwing System.LimitException: Too many SOQL queries: 101 only on days when the batch's Account Data Loader import ran first. Walk through how you'd diagnose and fix this.
questions.modelAnswer: The number 101 is the giveaway -- it's exactly one past the 100 synchronous SOQL query limit, which strongly suggests a query inside a loop that's firing one extra time than usual, not a query count that scales wildly out of control. The fact that it only happens on days the Account Data Loader import ran first points to a trigger or automation on Account (fired by that import) that, through a workflow rule, process builder, or flow, updates related Contacts, which re-enters the Contact automation and adds one additional query execution per Contact-triggering context that doesn't happen on a normal day. The fix starts with checking the debug log from a failing run and counting SOQL statements in the order they fired, to find the one that's inside a loop rather than hoisted above it; the fastest confirmation is usually finding a query executed inside a for loop over a trigger's record collection, bulkifying it by moving the query above the loop and building a lookup Map, which fixes the issue regardless of how many Contacts a given Data Loader batch happens to touch.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing that jumps out to me is 101 -- that's one over the sync limit of 100, which almost always means a query sitting inside a loop that fires once too many times relative to normal days, not something that scales unpredictably. The 'only after the Account import' detail tells me there's some automation on Account -- probably a flow or process builder -- that updates related Contacts as a side effect of that import, and that update is re-entering Contact-side logic that has a query inside a loop which normally doesn't get exercised, or doesn't get exercised at this volume, on a regular day. I'd pull the debug log from an actual failing run and literally count the SOQL statements in order -- that tells me exactly which query is the repeat offender. Once I find it, the fix is always the same: pull it out of the loop, batch the lookup with an IN clause into a Map, and do the per-record work against that map instead of hitting the database again inside the loop.
commonMistakes: Assuming the limit was just 'exceeded due to volume' without identifying the specific query-in-loop culprit
Not connecting the Account import trigger as the root cause of the extra automation re-entry
Not using the debug log to count actual SOQL statement order before guessing at a fix
Fixing symptoms (e.g. reducing batch size) instead of bulkifying the actual offending query

The Account import correlation suggests cross-object automation re-triggering Contact logic
Debug log review with a SOQL statement count pinpoints the exact offending query
The correct fix is bulkification: move the query above the loop, use a Map for lookups
