questions.title: Diagnosing a Mixed DML Error
questions.prompt: A Visualforce controller throws 'MIXED_DML_OPERATION, DML operation on setup object is not permitted after you have updated a non-setup object' when a user clicks a button that assigns a permission set and then updates a custom object record in the same transaction. Explain the cause and two different valid fixes.
questions.modelAnswer: Salesforce disallows mixing DML on setup objects (like PermissionSetAssignment, User, Group, or UserRole) with DML on non-setup objects (ordinary custom or standard business objects) within the same transaction, specifically because setup object changes can affect record-level security and visibility, and allowing both in one uncommitted transaction creates data-consistency risks around sharing recalculation mid-transaction. The error here is triggered because the code updates a non-setup custom object record and then performs a setup-object DML (assigning the PermissionSetAssignment) in the same execution context, and the order the error message calls out ('after you have updated a non-setup object') confirms the non-setup DML happened first. The cleanest fix is to move the setup-object DML into an asynchronous context -- wrapping the PermissionSetAssignment insert inside a @future(callout=false) method or a Queueable job -- since an async context starts a fresh transaction, separate from the one that already performed the non-setup DML. A second valid fix, if ordering can be controlled, is to perform the setup-object DML first, before any non-setup DML runs in that same synchronous transaction, since the restriction specifically fires on mixing in a transaction that has already touched a non-setup object; reordering avoids the conflict without needing an async hop.
questions.professionalAnswer: This error is really just Salesforce saying 'you touched a regular object and a setup object -- like a permission set assignment -- in the same transaction, and I won't allow that because setup objects affect security and visibility in ways that get complicated if they're changing mid-transaction with other data.' The message detail -- 'after you have updated a non-setup object' -- tells me the custom object update happened first and then the permission set assignment tried to run in that same still-open transaction. The fix I reach for most often is just pushing the setup-object DML into a @future method or a Queueable -- since that starts a genuinely separate transaction, there's nothing left to mix. If for some reason I can't go async there, the other option is just reordering the code so the permission set assignment happens first, before the custom object update runs -- since the restriction is specifically about a transaction that's already touched a non-setup object, doing the setup DML first sidesteps it entirely.
commonMistakes: Not knowing which objects count as 'setup objects' for this restriction (PermissionSetAssignment, User, Group, UserRole, etc.)
Proposing a fix that still mixes both DML types within the same synchronous transaction
Missing that an async context (future/Queueable) starts a genuinely separate transaction, resolving the conflict
Not considering the simpler reordering fix when async isn't appropriate
keyPoints: Setup objects (PermissionSetAssignment, User, Group, UserRole) can't be DML'd in the same transaction as non-setup objects
The restriction exists because setup changes affect security/sharing recalculation
Moving the setup-object DML to an async context (future/Queueable) resolves it via a separate transaction
Reordering so setup-object DML happens first, before any non-setup DML, is a second valid fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the mixed DML restriction and why it exists
Correctly diagnoses the specific cause from the error message's ordering detail
Gives the async-context fix correctly
Gives the reordering fix correctly as a valid alternative

questions.title: Trigger Recursion Sending Duplicate Emails
questions.prompt: Every time a Case is updated, the assigned agent receives the notification email three times instead of once. There's a single after-update trigger on Case that sends the email. What's the likely cause, and how do you confirm and fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: A single trigger firing the email three times for one user-initiated update strongly suggests recursion: the trigger (or logic it calls) performs a DML update on the same Case record, which re-triggers the after-update context, and if that update happens inside logic that doesn't check whether the email was already sent this transaction, each re-entry sends another copy. To confirm, checking the debug log's trigger execution trace will show the after-update trigger context firing more than once in a single transaction, with each firing's call stack showing it was invoked by a DML statement inside the trigger's own logic path (directly or via a flow/workflow field update the trigger itself caused) rather than by the original user action alone. The fix is a static recursion guard: a private static Boolean (or Set<Id> of already-processed record Ids) checked and set within the trigger handler, so the email-sending logic only executes once per actual top-level transaction regardless of how many times the trigger context re-fires as a side effect of its own update.
questions.professionalAnswer: Three exact copies for one real update is a classic recursion signature -- something in that trigger's own logic is doing a DML update on the Case, which re-fires the same after-update trigger, and if there's no guard, the email gets sent again every single time it re-enters. I'd confirm it by looking at the debug log and literally counting how many times the Case after-update context appears for one save -- if it's three, I've got my answer, and the call stack on each of those extra firings should point back to a DML inside the trigger's own code path, not a separate independent save. The fix is a static recursion guard -- a private static variable or a static Set of record Ids already processed in this transaction -- checked at the very top of the handler so the email only actually fires once no matter how many times this trigger context gets re-entered within the same transaction.
commonMistakes: Assuming the email provider or a workflow rule duplicate is the cause without checking trigger re-entry first
Not using the debug log's trigger execution trace to count actual firings
Fixing it by removing the DML that causes recursion instead of adding a proper recursion guard (when the DML is actually necessary)
Using an instance variable instead of a static variable for the guard, which resets on each re-entry and doesn't actually prevent recursion
keyPoints: Exact multiple-of-firing counts (three copies) is a strong recursion signature
Debug log trigger execution trace confirms the number of times the context actually fired
The trigger's own DML on the same record is the likely re-entry trigger
A static recursion guard (not an instance variable) correctly prevents the duplicate side effect

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses recursion as the likely cause
Describes a correct debugging method to confirm it (debug log trace)
Correctly specifies a static (not instance) recursion guard as the fix
Explains why the guard must be static to actually work

questions.title: A Batch Job Failing with CPU Time Limit Exceeded
questions.prompt: A Batch Apex job with a scope size of 200 starts throwing System.LimitException: Apex CPU time limit exceeded partway through a large run, but only on records added in the last month. What's your diagnostic approach and most likely fix?
questions.modelAnswer: Since the job worked fine on older records and only fails on recently-added ones, the likely cause is that something about those newer records increases the per-record CPU cost inside execute() -- commonly, a related child-record count that's grown (so a loop or nested logic that scales with child-record volume per Account/parent takes proportionally longer), a formula or validation evaluated per record that got more complex recently, or a nested query/logic path inside the loop that wasn't an issue when child volumes were smaller. The diagnostic approach is to isolate: run the batch manually with a very small scope size (say 5 or 10) against a handful of the specific failing recent records with debug logging enabled, and check the CPU time reported in the log's execution overview, then narrow down which specific operation inside execute() consumes the most time, often by adding targeted System.debug(Limits.getCpuTime()) checkpoints within the loop. The most likely fix, once the expensive per-record operation is identified, is either to move that heavy logic to an async follow-up job (chaining a Queueable from finish() for the records that need expensive processing) or to reduce the batch's scope size specifically for this job so the 60-second async CPU budget is spread across fewer records per execute() call, buying headroom without needing to optimize the logic itself immediately.
questions.professionalAnswer: The detail that jumps out is 'only on recent records,' because that means this isn't actually a batch-size problem, it's that something about those specific records is more expensive to process per-record than older ones were. My first move is to isolate it -- run the batch manually with a tiny scope size, like 5, against just a handful of the known-failing recent records with debug logging on, and look at what Limits.getCpuTime() shows me as I step through execute(). Nine times out of ten this turns out to be something like a nested loop over a growing number of child records, or a calculation that's gotten heavier recently and happens to apply mostly to newer data. Once I know exactly which line is burning the CPU, I've got two real options -- either push that specific expensive piece off into its own async job so it's not competing for budget inside this batch's execute() call, or just drop the scope size down so each execute() call has fewer records splitting that 60-second budget, buying time while I actually fix the underlying logic properly.

Not isolating the specific operation inside execute() causing the CPU cost
Not using Limits.getCpuTime() checkpoints or debug logs to pinpoint the actual expensive logic
Treating this as a volume problem rather than a per-record cost problem specific to recent data
keyPoints: The 'only recent records' detail points to a per-record cost increase, not raw volume
Isolate with a small scope size and debug logging/Limits.getCpuTime() checkpoints to find the expensive operation
Likely causes: growing related-record counts, heavier calculations, or nested logic scaling with recent data
Fix options: move the expensive logic to a follow-up async job, or reduce scope size as a stopgap

Describes a correct, methodical isolation/debugging approach

questions.title: An LWC That Shows Stale Data After an Update
questions.prompt: A Lightning Web Component shows an Opportunity's Amount using @wire(getRecord), and a separate custom button updates that Amount via an imperative Apex call. After clicking the button, the displayed Amount doesn't refresh until the whole page is manually reloaded. Diagnose and fix this.
questions.modelAnswer: getRecord reads from the shared Lightning Data Service cache, and that cache only refreshes automatically when a change happens through an LDS-aware path -- another getRecord-based component's record edit via lightning-record-edit-form, or notifyRecordUpdateAvailable/refreshApex-style signals. An imperative Apex call that performs the update server-side bypasses LDS entirely; the platform has no way of knowing the underlying record changed, because from LDS's perspective, nothing it's aware of initiated that write, so the cached value the wired getRecord is still showing is now stale. The fix is to explicitly tell LDS to refresh its cache for that record after the imperative Apex call succeeds, using the lightning/uiRecordApi module's refreshRecord (or more simply, re-wiring with @wire and calling refreshApex on the wired result if using a wired, not imperative, Apex call) -- calling refreshRecord(recordId) or the equivalent after the imperative update's promise resolves tells LDS to re-fetch and propagate the fresh value, which will automatically update every component (including this one) displaying that record through the LDS cache.
questions.professionalAnswer: The root of this is that getRecord is reading from LDS's shared cache, and LDS only knows to refresh that cache when the write happens through a path it's aware of. An imperative Apex call is exactly the kind of write LDS has no visibility into -- it just updated the database directly, with LDS none the wiser, so the cached value this component is still displaying is now out of date and nothing's told it otherwise. The fix is to explicitly refresh the record after that imperative call resolves -- importing refreshRecord from lightning/uiRecordApi and calling it with the recordId once my Apex promise comes back successfully. Once I do that, LDS re-fetches the record and every component on the page reading that same record through getRecord updates automatically, not just this one -- which is actually the nice side effect of fixing it this way instead of, say, manually re-querying inside just this one component.

Fixing it by manually re-querying with an imperative Apex call inside this component instead of refreshing the shared LDS cache
Not knowing refreshRecord from lightning/uiRecordApi exists for exactly this purpose
Forcing a full page reload as the 'fix' instead of addressing the cache refresh properly

An imperative Apex write bypasses LDS entirely, leaving the cache stale with no automatic signal
refreshRecord (lightning/uiRecordApi) explicitly tells LDS to re-fetch and propagate the fresh value
Refreshing via LDS updates every component on the page displaying that record, not just one

questions.title: A Non-Selective Report Filter Timing Out
questions.prompt: A report on a custom object with 2 million records, filtered on a custom text field 'Region__c', times out for most users but runs fine for a System Administrator. Diagnose why, and propose a real fix.
questions.modelAnswer: Region__c is a custom text field, which Salesforce does not index by default, so filtering 2 million records on it is a non-selective query that has to scan a large percentage of the table -- Salesforce's query optimizer chooses between an indexed path and a full-table-scan-like path based on estimated selectivity, and an admin's broader data visibility combined with the platform occasionally applying different query plans or timeout tolerances for certain profiles can make this appear to 'work for the admin' while timing out for regular users, though the real underlying issue is the same non-selective filter for everyone -- it's just more likely to manifest as an outright timeout for users whose queries additionally have to apply sharing-rule-based row-level security filtering on top of the already-expensive scan, which adds further overhead admins (who see everything, bypassing most sharing checks) don't incur. The real fix is making Region__c selective: either request a custom index on it via a Salesforce support case if filtering by Region is a common, business-critical access pattern, or, more simply, convert Region__c to a picklist and use standard picklist-based filtering combined with a more selective combination of filters (adding a second, naturally more selective filter like a date range or owner), since a custom index case can take time to provision and isn't always feasible immediately. Longer term, if the object is approaching or exceeding LDV thresholds, this is also a sign the object's indexing/archival strategy needs a broader review, not just a one-off fix for this report.
questions.professionalAnswer: The giveaway for me is that it's a custom text field with no index behind it, on an object with two million rows -- that's a textbook non-selective filter, and at that scale it's exactly the kind of thing that times out. Why it 'works for the admin' is really just that the admin's broader visibility and different effective query path make the practical timeout less likely to trip for them specifically, even though the underlying filter is just as unselective for everyone -- regular users are also paying the cost of sharing-rule row-level filtering stacked on top of that same expensive scan, which tips them over the edge. The real fix isn't 'give everyone admin access,' obviously -- it's making Region__c actually selective. If Region really is a bounded set of values, I'd first ask why it's a free-text field at all instead of a picklist, since picklist-based filtering combined with a second selective filter, like a date range, often gets you there without needing anything exotic. If that's not enough and this report pattern is business-critical, I'd open a support case to request a custom index on the field directly -- that's the real, durable fix for a genuinely high-volume, frequently-filtered custom field.
commonMistakes: Assuming the admin-works/user-fails difference means it's a permissions bug rather than a selectivity problem
Not identifying the unindexed custom text field as the root selectivity issue
Proposing 'give users more access' instead of addressing the underlying query selectivity
Missing that sharing-rule row-level filtering adds additional overhead for regular (non-admin) users on top of the scan
keyPoints: Region__c as an unindexed custom text field is a non-selective filter at 2 million rows
Admin visibility differences and sharing-rule overhead explain why it appears to work only for the admin
Real fixes: convert to a picklist, add a second selective filter, or request a custom index via support
This is also a signal to review the object's broader LDV indexing/archival strategy

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the unindexed custom text field as the root selectivity problem
Correctly explains why the admin case appears to work despite the same underlying issue
Proposes concrete, correct remediation options
Connects this to broader LDV considerations

questions.title: A SOQL Query Returning Fewer Records Than Expected Due to Sharing
questions.prompt: An integration user's Apex REST service returns far fewer Opportunity records than the external system expects, even though the query's WHERE clause looks correct and the records definitely exist. What's the most likely cause, and what are the two different ways to address it?
questions.modelAnswer: Apex classes run in the context of the calling user's sharing rules by default (with sharing or no explicit sharing keyword defaults to inheriting the caller's sharing context in most cases, but a class explicitly declared without sharing ignores record-level sharing entirely in the other direction), so if the Apex REST endpoint's controller class is declared with sharing, any Opportunity the integration user's profile and sharing rules don't grant visibility to is silently excluded from the query results -- the WHERE clause's business logic is correct, but the user simply can't see those rows, and SOQL doesn't throw an error for that, it just omits rows. The two valid fixes are: first, grant the integration user broader actual record access through proper sharing rules, a permission set, or role hierarchy placement, so their visibility genuinely matches what the integration is supposed to return -- the more correct long-term fix when the integration is meant to represent a real business user's legitimate access. Second, if the integration is deliberately meant to operate with elevated, system-level visibility regardless of the calling user's own record access (common for a true system-to-system integration context), declare the controller class without sharing, which runs the query in system context and bypasses sharing rules entirely -- though this should be a deliberate architectural decision, documented, since it widens what the integration can see beyond the calling user's actual access.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd check is the sharing keyword on the Apex class behind that REST endpoint, because if it's declared with sharing, the query is running inside that integration user's own record-level visibility -- and if their profile, role, or sharing rules don't grant them access to some of those Opportunities, SOQL just quietly leaves those rows out, no error, nothing to make this obvious except 'fewer records than expected.' Once I confirm that's the cause, I've got two legitimate ways to fix it, and which one's right depends on intent. If this integration user is supposed to represent real business-level access, the correct fix is actually giving them proper access -- a permission set, sharing rule, or role placement that reflects what they should legitimately see. If this is meant to be a genuine system-level integration that should see everything regardless of any one user's sharing context, then the class should be without sharing, which runs in system mode and bypasses sharing entirely -- but I'd treat that as a real architectural decision to document, not just a quick fix, because it does mean the integration sees more than that user's normal access would ever allow.
commonMistakes: Assuming a query bug or wrong WHERE clause logic instead of checking the sharing context first
Not knowing SOQL silently omits inaccessible rows rather than throwing an error
Jumping straight to 'without sharing' without considering whether proper access (permission set/sharing rule) is the more correct fix
Treating 'without sharing' as a trivial fix rather than a deliberate, documented architectural decision
keyPoints: Apex classes declared with sharing enforce the calling user's record-level sharing on queries
SOQL silently omits rows the running user can't see -- no error is thrown
Fix 1: grant the integration user genuine access via permission set/sharing rule/role
Fix 2: declare the class without sharing for deliberate system-level visibility, documented as an architectural choice

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies sharing context as the root cause
Correctly explains SOQL's silent row omission behavior
Correctly describes the 'grant real access' fix
Correctly describes the 'without sharing' fix and its architectural implications

questions.title: Debugging Duplicate Rows from a SOQL Relationship Query
questions.prompt: A SOQL query joining Opportunity to OpportunityLineItem via a parent-to-child subquery, flattened in Apex into a single list for a report, is producing what looks like duplicate Opportunity rows. Diagnose the likely cause and the correct fix.
questions.modelAnswer: The SOQL query itself, structured as a parent-to-child subquery, is not capable of producing duplicate parent rows -- each Opportunity appears exactly once in the outer result, with its OpportunityLineItems correctly nested as a sub-list on that single Opportunity object. What looks like duplicate Opportunity rows is almost always a bug in the Apex flattening logic: if the code iterates the nested line-item list and, inside that inner loop, also appends the parent Opportunity itself to a separate flat output list (rather than only building one combined report row per line item, which legitimately repeats Opportunity-level fields across multiple rows by design), the Opportunity ends up added once per line item it has, which looks like duplication but is actually a double-counting bug in the flattening code, not the query. The fix is to carefully separate 'one flattened report row per line item, with Opportunity fields repeated across rows' (which is correct and expected for a line-item-level report) from any logic that separately and redundantly tracks or outputs the parent Opportunity itself inside that same inner loop.
questions.professionalAnswer: The query itself can't actually produce duplicate parent rows this way -- a parent-to-child subquery gives you each Opportunity exactly once, with its line items nested underneath it as a sub-list, full stop. So when this looks like duplicates, I'm not debugging SOQL, I'm debugging whatever Apex loop is flattening that nested result into a report list. Nine times out of ten, what's actually happening is someone's inner loop over the line items is also, separately, appending the parent Opportunity to some other flat list -- which means the Opportunity gets added once per line item it has, and if an Opportunity has four line items, it looks like it duplicated four times. That's not a duplicate, technically -- each row genuinely does represent one line item with its parent's fields repeated, which is normal and expected for a line-item-level report -- the actual bug is if there's additional logic separately double-counting or re-adding the Opportunity itself on top of that, which is what I'd go hunting for in the flattening code, not the query.
commonMistakes: Blaming the SOQL query itself for producing duplicate parent rows, when the subquery structure can't do that
Not distinguishing 'expected row-per-line-item repetition' from an actual double-counting bug
Not inspecting the Apex loop that flattens the nested result as the actual place to look for the bug
Rewriting the query (e.g. switching to two separate queries) instead of fixing the flattening logic
keyPoints: A parent-to-child SOQL subquery cannot itself produce duplicate parent rows
Apparent duplication is almost always a bug in the Apex code flattening the nested result
One report row per line item, repeating Opportunity fields, is correct and expected for a line-item report
The real bug to find is separate, redundant logic re-adding the parent inside the line-item loop

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly rules out the SOQL query itself as the cause
Correctly identifies the Apex flattening logic as the likely bug location
Distinguishes expected row repetition from an actual double-counting bug
Proposes a sensible, targeted fix

questions.title: A CRM Analytics Dataflow Failing at the Sync Step
questions.prompt: A CRM Analytics dataflow that has run successfully every night for months suddenly fails at its initial sync (digest) node, with an error referencing a field that no longer exists. What's your diagnostic process and fix?
questions.modelAnswer: A dataflow failing specifically at the digest/sync node with an error naming a missing field almost always means a Salesforce-side schema change -- a field was deleted, renamed, or its API name changed (for example, during a managed package upgrade or a cleanup project) -- broke the dataflow's hardcoded reference to that field in its JSON definition, since dataflows reference specific field API names directly and have no automatic schema-drift tolerance. The diagnostic process starts by checking the exact field API name in the error against Salesforce setup (Object Manager) to confirm whether it was deleted, renamed, or is simply unavailable to the running user context (a profile/permission change removing field-level security access would produce a similar-looking failure). The fix depends on which of those it is: if the field was genuinely removed or renamed, the dataflow's digest node JSON needs to be updated to reference the correct current field (or have that field recreated if deletion was unintentional); if it's an FLS/access issue instead, the running user (the one whose context the dataflow executes under) needs the field access restored, since dataflows execute with a specific running user's permissions, not always directly the admin who built it.
questions.professionalAnswer: A sudden failure after months of success, specifically at the digest step and specifically naming a field, tells me this isn't a data problem, it's a schema-drift problem -- something changed on the Salesforce side that this dataflow's JSON wasn't updated for, most likely a field that got deleted or renamed, sometimes as a side effect of a package upgrade or someone doing object cleanup without checking dependencies first. My first move is just going to Object Manager and checking whether that exact field API name still exists at all -- if it's gone or renamed, that confirms the cause immediately. The other thing I always check, because it looks identical from the error, is whether the dataflow's running user still has field-level security access to that field -- a permission change can produce the exact same symptom even though the field itself is fine. Once I know which of those two it is, the fix is either updating the dataflow's digest node to point at the correct current field, or restoring that running user's FLS access -- but either way, the real lesson here is that nobody checked dataflow dependencies before making that Salesforce-side change, which is the process gap I'd actually flag afterward.
commonMistakes: Assuming it's a dataflow platform bug rather than a Salesforce-side schema or access change
Not checking whether the field was deleted/renamed versus an FLS/access issue, which look similar
Fixing the symptom by recreating the field without understanding why it was changed in the first place
Not flagging the underlying process gap (no dependency check before schema changes)
keyPoints: Dataflows reference field API names directly with no automatic schema-drift tolerance
Check Object Manager to confirm whether the field was deleted, renamed, or access-restricted
FLS/access changes on the dataflow's running user can look identical to a true schema change
The real process fix is checking dataflow/recipe dependencies before making Salesforce-side schema changes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies schema drift as the likely root cause
Describes a correct diagnostic process distinguishing deletion/rename from FLS access
Proposes a correct fix for either scenario
Identifies the underlying process gap worth addressing

questions.title: A Data Export Accidentally Exposing PII
questions.prompt: A scheduled report export to a shared drive, used by a marketing team for years, is discovered to include a Social Security Number custom field that was added to the underlying report type last quarter without anyone reviewing the export's downstream destination. What do you do, in order, once this is discovered?
questions.modelAnswer: The immediate first step is to stop the bleeding: disable or pause the scheduled export so no further files containing the SSN field land on the shared drive while the situation is assessed, and restrict access to the shared drive location (or at minimum the specific files already there) to the smallest group needed for remediation, not the marketing team's normal broad access. Next, determine actual exposure scope -- how many export files exist, how long the field has been included (since last quarter, per the scenario), and who has had access to that shared drive location during that window -- because the remediation and any required notification obligations depend entirely on real exposure, not assumption. In parallel, fix the root cause: remove the SSN field from the underlying report type (or report) so it can never again flow into that export, and review whether any other report type changes in the same period introduced similar unreviewed sensitive-field exposure elsewhere. Depending on the organization's data classification policy and applicable regulations, this likely needs escalation to security/compliance/legal to assess whether a breach notification obligation exists, since unintentional SSN exposure to an internal team without a need-to-know can trigger legal reporting requirements depending on jurisdiction and how broadly the shared drive was actually accessible. Finally, the process fix going forward is a governance gap: report type field changes that touch sensitive/classified fields need a review step before fields can flow into existing scheduled exports, not just ad hoc trust that whoever adds a field checks every downstream consumer.
questions.professionalAnswer: First thing I do is stop the export and lock down access to whatever's already on that shared drive -- not to hide it, but because every additional day it sits there with broad access is more exposure, and that has to stop immediately before anything else. Then I actually need to know the real scope -- how many files, how far back, who actually had access to that drive location during that window -- because what happens next depends entirely on real exposure, not on my guess at it. At the same time, I'd pull the SSN field back out of that report type so it physically can't flow into this export again, and I'd check whether other reports changed around the same time might have the same unreviewed-sensitive-field problem. Given this is SSN specifically, I'm not making the call myself on whether this needs to be reported as a breach -- that goes to security, compliance, and legal immediately, because unintentional exposure of something like SSNs can carry real notification obligations depending on who actually had access and for how long. And once the immediate fire's out, the thing I'd push hardest on afterward is the actual process gap -- there was no review step catching a sensitive field getting added to a report type that already fed a long-standing export, and that's what has to change so this doesn't just happen again with a different field next quarter.
commonMistakes: Focusing only on the technical fix (removing the field) without addressing immediate access/exposure containment first
Not determining actual exposure scope before deciding on next steps
Making a unilateral call on breach notification obligations instead of escalating to security/compliance/legal
Not addressing the underlying governance gap that let a sensitive field reach an export unreviewed
keyPoints: Immediate containment first: pause the export and restrict access to existing exposed files
Determine real exposure scope (how long, how many files, who had access) before further action
Remove the sensitive field from the report type to fix the root cause
Escalate to security/compliance/legal for breach notification assessment rather than deciding unilaterally
Address the governance gap: sensitive-field changes need review before flowing into existing exports

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly prioritizes immediate containment before other steps
Correctly determines exposure scope before deciding next actions
Correctly escalates compliance/legal risk instead of deciding unilaterally
Addresses the underlying governance process gap

questions.title: A Platform Event Subscriber Silently Missing Events
questions.prompt: An external system subscribed to a custom Platform Event via CometD reports it's missing roughly 5% of events during peak hours, with no errors on the Salesforce side. What's the likely cause, and how do you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: Platform Events are retained for a limited replay window (24 hours standard, extendable with add-on event storage), and a subscriber using CometD needs to explicitly manage its replay ID and request replay from a specific point if its connection drops, reconnects, or falls behind during a high-volume burst; a subscriber that simply reconnects and resumes from -1 (new events only) after a disconnect, rather than replaying from its last successfully-processed replay ID, will silently miss every event published during the gap, which matches a pattern of missing events specifically during peak hours when connection drops or processing backpressure are most likely. A second common cause is the subscriber's own processing throughput falling behind the publish rate during a burst, causing its client-side buffer to drop or skip events rather than queueing them durably, if the client implementation isn't correctly using the durable replay mechanism at all. The fix is ensuring the subscriber persists the last successfully processed replayId durably (outside in-memory state that's lost on reconnect) and, on reconnect, explicitly requests replay starting from that stored replayId rather than defaulting to -1, which replays only new events and skips the gap; if peak-hour volume genuinely exceeds what a single CometD client can keep up with, adding consumer concurrency or moving to the Pub/Sub API (gRPC-based, generally more efficient for high-throughput subscription) is the scaling fix.
questions.professionalAnswer: Missing events specifically during peak hours, with nothing wrong on the Salesforce side, points me straight at how the subscriber is handling reconnects and replay, not at Salesforce dropping anything. Platform Events have a replay window, and the whole point of a replayId is that a subscriber that gets disconnected -- which is exactly what's more likely to happen under peak load -- should reconnect and ask to replay starting from the last replayId it actually processed. If their client is coded to just reconnect and resume from -1, meaning 'only give me new events from now on,' every event published during that disconnect gap is gone for them, silently, with nothing on our side indicating a problem because the events were published successfully. I'd ask them to confirm they're persisting the last processed replayId somewhere durable, outside of just an in-memory variable that disappears on reconnect, and that they're explicitly requesting replay from that stored value, not defaulting to new-events-only. If their actual processing throughput is the bottleneck, not just reconnects, then it's a scaling conversation -- more consumer concurrency, or moving them onto the Pub/Sub API, which handles high-throughput subscription more efficiently than classic CometD.
commonMistakes: Assuming Salesforce is dropping or failing to publish events without checking the subscriber's replay handling first
Not knowing Platform Events have a limited replay retention window
Missing that a subscriber resuming from -1 after a disconnect skips every event published during the gap
Not distinguishing a replay-handling bug from a genuine throughput/scaling bottleneck
keyPoints: Platform Events have a limited replay retention window (24 hours standard)
A subscriber must persist its last processed replayId durably and request replay from it on reconnect
Resuming from -1 after a disconnect silently skips every event published during the gap
Genuine throughput bottlenecks are a separate scaling issue, addressed with concurrency or the Pub/Sub API

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies subscriber-side replay handling as the likely root cause
Correctly explains the replayId/reconnect mechanism and the -1 pitfall
Distinguishes this from a genuine Salesforce-side publishing failure
Proposes a correct fix including the scaling alternative

questions.title: Diagnosing and Fixing an Org-Wide Slowdown from Unmanaged Large Data Volume Growth
questions.prompt: Over the past year, an Opportunity object has grown to 8 million records with no archiving strategy. List views are timing out, nightly batch jobs are missing their windows, and reports time out for most users. As the architect brought in to fix this, walk through your full diagnosis and remediation plan.
questions.modelAnswer: A real LDV remediation starts by confirming the cause is genuinely volume-driven rather than a disguised configuration bug, then systematically auditing query selectivity across the hot paths causing timeouts, designing an archiving strategy (Big Objects, an external warehouse, or simple date-exclusion) for data that no longer needs to live in active core storage, fixing batch job scope and scheduling, and finally establishing an ongoing data lifecycle policy so this doesn't recur. See the deep-dive walkthrough for the full diagnostic and remediation sequence.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through this exactly the way the deep dive lays it out -- confirm it's real LDV first, not a filter bug wearing an LDV costume, then audit selectivity, then design the archive, then fix the batch scheduling, then put guardrails in so I'm not back here in another year. See the deep-dive sections for how I'd actually run each of those steps.
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to an expensive archiving project without first ruling out a cheaper configuration bug as the actual cause
Treating selectivity auditing and archiving as interchangeable fixes instead of complementary, sequential steps
Proposing deletion of old records without checking legal/compliance retention requirements first
Fixing the immediate timeouts without establishing an ongoing lifecycle policy to prevent recurrence
Not reviewing whether batch job scheduling collisions, not just individual job runtime, caused missed windows
keyPoints: Confirm genuine LDV causation before committing to an archiving project
Systematically audit and fix non-selective query filters across hot paths first
Design an archive strategy (Big Objects, external warehouse, or date-exclusion) with real business/compliance sign-off
Address batch job selectivity, scope size, and scheduling collisions separately from report/list view fixes
Establish an ongoing data lifecycle policy and selectivity review gate to prevent recurrence

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes genuine LDV causation from a configuration bug before proceeding
Proposes a correct, systematic selectivity audit and remediation
Designs a sound archiving strategy with correct tool choices and compliance awareness
Correctly addresses batch job scope/scheduling as a related but distinct problem
Proposes durable guardrails to prevent recurrence, not just a one-time fix

deepDive.heading: Confirm this is genuinely an LDV problem, not a configuration bug
deepDive.content: Before assuming raw volume is the cause, rule out the cheaper, more common explanations first: check whether any of the failing list views or reports use non-selective filters on unindexed custom fields (a filter bug that would cause the same symptoms at a much lower record count), check whether a recently added trigger, flow, or roll-up summary is adding per-record overhead that didn't exist before, and check whether sharing rule complexity (a large number of criteria-based sharing rules recalculating on every save) has grown alongside the data. If none of those explain the timing -- the slowdown correlates with the object crossing roughly the multi-million-row threshold and the queries in question are genuinely non-selective at that scale -- then this is a real LDV problem, not a configuration regression masquerading as one, and the remediation plan below applies. Conflating the two is the single biggest risk at this stage: treating a configuration bug as an LDV problem leads to an expensive archiving project that doesn't actually fix the real cause.

deepDive.heading: Audit indexing and query selectivity across the hot paths
deepDive.content: List every report, list view, and batch job filter condition touching Opportunity and classify each as selective (filtering on an indexed field: Id, Name, CreatedDate, OwnerId, a lookup field, or an External ID/unique custom field) or non-selective (an unindexed custom text/picklist/checkbox field, or a filter combination the query optimizer can't use an index for even if individual fields are indexed). For every non-selective hot path that's business-critical, the fix is either converting the filtered field to one of the auto-indexed types, requesting a custom index on it via a Salesforce support case, or restructuring the filter to combine with a genuinely selective field so the combined filter crosses the platform's selectivity threshold. This audit alone frequently resolves the majority of timeouts, because in practice most LDV slowdowns trace back to a handful of specific non-selective filters repeated across many reports, not an un-fixable platform ceiling.

deepDive.heading: Design the archiving strategy for records that no longer need to live in core storage
deepDive.content: Work with the business to define a genuine archival policy -- for example, Closed Won/Closed Lost Opportunities older than 24 months rarely need to be queried in day-to-day operational reports or list views, and can be moved out of core Salesforce storage. The options, in order of typical preference: Salesforce Big Objects for data that needs to remain queryable within Salesforce at huge scale with simple key-based access patterns; an external archive (a data warehouse like Snowflake, populated via Bulk API extracts) for data primarily needed for historical reporting/BI rather than transactional Salesforce UI access; or, for data that must stay in Salesforce but rarely needs to be queried, simply ensuring it's excluded from the hot-path reports and list views via date-based filters so it isn't actively dragging down every query even though it still physically exists in the object. The business sign-off on what 'no longer needs to live in active storage' means is the actual hard part here, not the technical migration -- legal/compliance retention requirements often mean records can't simply be deleted even once they're archived out of active query paths.

deepDive.heading: Fix the batch job scheduling and scope
deepDive.content: For the batch jobs missing their windows, apply the same selectivity audit to their query locators first, since a non-selective start() query is often the single biggest contributor to a batch job's total runtime growing over the past year. Beyond selectivity, reduce scope size for batches whose per-record logic is doing nontrivial work, since a smaller scope size trades more chunks for less CPU/DML pressure per chunk and can resolve CPU-time failures without re-architecting the job. Finally, review whether multiple batch/scheduled jobs are now colliding in their execution windows as data volume has grown job runtimes longer than originally scheduled -- staggering schedules or consolidating overlapping jobs is often necessary once volume has grown enough that a job that used to finish in 20 minutes now takes two hours.

deepDive.heading: Put guardrails in place so this doesn't recur
deepDive.content: The root organizational failure here wasn't the data volume itself, it was the absence of a standing archiving policy that should have been established well before 8 million rows. Going forward: define a data lifecycle policy per major object (how long records stay in active storage, what happens after that), add volume and query-performance monitoring (not just waiting for users to report timeouts), and require that any new report, list view, or filter added against a known-large object go through a selectivity review before shipping, the same way a code review gates logic changes. This turns LDV management from a reactive fire drill into a routine, owned part of the architecture practice.

questions.title: Multi-Org vs. Single-Org: The Real Decision Criteria
questions.prompt: A growing company with three regional business units, each with somewhat different sales processes, is debating a single global Salesforce org versus separate orgs per region. What criteria actually drive this decision, beyond 'single org is simpler'?
questions.modelAnswer: A single org is the right default when the business units need to report on consolidated, cross-region data (a global pipeline view, shared customer records across regions), when integration complexity would otherwise multiply (each additional org means separate integration endpoints, separate master data, and separate sync logic to keep customer/product data consistent), and when the process differences between regions can be accommodated through record types, page layouts, and profile-based customization rather than needing genuinely incompatible data models. Separate orgs become justified when regulatory data residency requirements legally mandate data separation by region (common in certain financial services or government contexts), when the business units are functionally near-independent with no real cross-region reporting need and minimal customer overlap, or when org-level limits (API call limits, data storage, feature-license boundaries) are genuinely being approached by combined usage in ways a single org's limits can't absorb. The 'differing sales processes' detail alone is rarely sufficient justification for multiple orgs, since Salesforce's record type and page layout framework is specifically built to let meaningfully different processes coexist cleanly on the same underlying data model within one org.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first question is always whether leadership actually needs one consolidated, real-time view across all three regions -- a single global pipeline report, one customer record visible company-wide -- because if the honest answer is yes, that's an enormous point in favor of a single org, since multiple orgs means building and maintaining real integration just to stitch that view back together artificially. Different sales processes by themselves don't really move me toward multiple orgs -- record types and page layouts exist specifically so meaningfully different processes can live cleanly in one org without stepping on each other. What actually pushes me toward separate orgs is something structural -- a real data residency law that legally requires separation, genuinely minimal customer or data overlap between the regions with no cross-reporting need at all, or org-level limits that combined usage is realistically going to hit. Short of one of those, I'd push hard for a single org and solve the process differences declaratively, because the integration tax of running multiple orgs is almost always underestimated at decision time and overpaid for years afterward.
commonMistakes: Treating differing sales processes alone as sufficient justification for separate orgs
Not weighing the ongoing integration/master-data-sync cost of a multi-org approach
Missing genuine drivers like data residency regulation or real org-limit constraints
Assuming 'simpler to manage separately' without accounting for cross-org reporting complexity created
keyPoints: Single org is favored when cross-region consolidated reporting/data sharing is a real business need
Record types and page layouts handle differing processes within one org in most cases
Genuine drivers for separate orgs: data residency law, real org-limit constraints, true business independence
Multi-org creates an ongoing integration/master-data-sync cost that's frequently underestimated

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies cross-region reporting/data needs as the primary decision driver
Correctly explains that differing processes alone don't justify multiple orgs
Names genuine, concrete drivers that do justify multiple orgs
Addresses the ongoing integration cost of a multi-org approach

questions.title: Designing Sharing Architecture for a Territory-Based Sales Org
questions.prompt: A sales org with 400 reps organized into overlapping territories (a rep can belong to more than one territory, and territories can span regions) needs record-level sharing on Accounts that matches territory membership, not the standard role hierarchy. What architecture do you propose?
questions.modelAnswer: The overlapping-membership requirement (a rep in more than one territory) rules out the standard role hierarchy as the primary access mechanism, since role hierarchy models a strict tree where each user has exactly one position, not a many-to-many membership structure. Salesforce's purpose-built answer is Enterprise Territory Management (ETM), which models territories as a hierarchy that can have many-to-many associations with both Accounts (via territory assignment rules or manual assignment) and Users (a user can be assigned to multiple territories), and automatically grants the configured level of access (read or read/write) to users for Accounts assigned to any territory they belong to. The OWD for Account should remain Private as the baseline, with ETM's territory-based access layered on top as the primary access-granting mechanism rather than relying on criteria-based sharing rules to simulate territory overlap, since criteria-based sharing rules would require significant custom criteria logic to replicate what ETM already models natively and would be much harder to maintain as territory definitions and rep assignments change over time. For any case ETM's assignment rules can't fully express (a one-off manual account-to-rep exception, for instance), targeted manual sharing or a narrowly-scoped additional sharing rule can supplement ETM without replacing it as the primary mechanism.
questions.professionalAnswer: The overlapping-membership detail is the key signal here -- a rep belonging to multiple territories at once means the role hierarchy, which only gives each user one position in a strict tree, just isn't the right tool for this on its own. This is exactly the scenario Enterprise Territory Management was built for -- it lets territories have a many-to-many relationship with both Accounts and Users, so a rep assigned to two territories automatically gets access to every Account assigned into either of those territories, without me trying to hand-build that overlap logic myself through a pile of criteria-based sharing rules. I'd keep OWD on Account at Private as the floor, and let ETM's territory assignment rules be the real access-granting mechanism layered on top, rather than trying to simulate territory membership through sharing rule criteria, which would turn into an unmaintainable mess the moment territory definitions change, which they always do. If there's a genuine one-off exception ETM's rules can't capture, I'd handle that with a narrow, specific manual share rather than bending the whole architecture around an edge case.
commonMistakes: Proposing role hierarchy as the primary mechanism despite the many-to-many membership requirement
Trying to simulate territory overlap entirely through complex criteria-based sharing rules instead of using ETM
Not keeping OWD at a restrictive baseline (Private) with ETM layered on top
Over-engineering manual sharing for cases ETM's native assignment rules already handle
keyPoints: Role hierarchy can't model many-to-many territory membership; ETM is the purpose-built mechanism
ETM supports many-to-many Account and User territory associations with native access-level configuration
OWD stays Private as the baseline, with ETM as the primary access-granting layer
Manual sharing or targeted sharing rules should supplement, not replace, ETM for true edge cases

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies ETM as the appropriate mechanism for overlapping territory membership
Correctly explains why role hierarchy alone doesn't fit this requirement
Correctly recommends Private OWD with ETM layered on top
Appropriately scopes manual sharing/sharing rules to true edge cases only

questions.title: A CI/CD Pipeline Design for a Growing Salesforce DX Team
questions.prompt: A team of six developers is moving from change-set-based deployments to a proper Salesforce DX CI/CD pipeline using unlocked packages. Design the pipeline, including what gates a change before it reaches production.
questions.modelAnswer: The pipeline should be source-driven end to end: each developer works in their own scratch org created from a shared project-scratch-def.json, builds and tests a feature there, and commits source-controlled metadata (not org-direct changes) to a feature branch. A pull request into the integration branch triggers a CI job that spins up a fresh scratch org, deploys the PR's source, and runs the full Apex test suite (enforcing the org-wide minimum 75% code coverage requirement as a floor, with a higher team-set bar like 85% as an actual quality gate) plus any static analysis (PMD or similar) configured for the project; a failing test suite or coverage shortfall blocks the merge. Once merged to the integration branch, the pipeline builds a new version of the unlocked package, deploys it to a dedicated QA/staging sandbox for manual or automated UAT, and only after that validation passes does the pipeline promote the specific package version to production via a scripted package install (not a change set), which keeps production deployments fully reproducible and auditable against a specific, versioned package build rather than an ad hoc bundle of whatever metadata happened to be in a change set at export time. Rollback is handled by having the previous package version readily available to reinstall, which is one of the real advantages of package-based deployment over change sets.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd want every developer working in their own scratch org, spun up from the same shared scratch-org-def file so nobody's working against a drifted baseline, and everything they do gets committed as source, not clicked into an org directly. A pull request into our integration branch is the real gate -- that's where CI spins up a disposable scratch org, deploys just that PR's code, and runs the full Apex test suite, and I'd set our actual bar above Salesforce's bare 75% minimum, closer to 85%, because 75% is a platform floor, not a quality target. Once something's merged, the pipeline builds an actual versioned unlocked package and that's what moves through a QA sandbox for real validation, and only a specific, already-validated package version gets promoted to production -- never a change set, because a change set isn't a reproducible artifact the way a versioned package is. The nice side effect of doing it this way is rollback is just reinstalling the previous package version, which is a lot more reliable than trying to reverse-engineer what a change set actually changed after the fact.
commonMistakes: Keeping change-set-based production deployment instead of moving to versioned package installs
Treating 75% code coverage as the quality bar instead of the platform's bare compliance floor
Not using a shared scratch org definition file, allowing environment drift between developers
No clear rollback strategy beyond 'figure it out when something breaks'
keyPoints: Scratch orgs from a shared definition file keep every developer's environment consistent
PR-triggered CI running the full test suite with a real quality bar (above the 75% floor) gates merges
Production deployment uses a versioned unlocked package install, not a change set
Rollback is reinstalling a previous validated package version, a real advantage of package-based deployment

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs the scratch-org and source-control workflow
Correctly designs the PR/CI gate including testing and a real quality bar
Correctly uses versioned unlocked package installs for production deployment
Addresses rollback strategy

questions.title: Designing a Sandbox and Release Cadence Strategy
questions.prompt: An org currently has one full-copy sandbox that every developer and QA shares, causing constant collisions and stale test data. Propose a proper sandbox strategy and release cadence for a team of eight.
questions.modelAnswer: The right structure separates concerns by sandbox type and purpose rather than everyone sharing one environment: individual developers work in their own scratch orgs (or Developer sandboxes if scratch orgs aren't fully adopted yet) for feature-level work, isolating their changes entirely from everyone else's; a shared Developer Pro or partial-copy Integration sandbox serves as the place feature branches merge together for cross-feature integration testing before QA; a dedicated QA/UAT sandbox (partial or full copy, refreshed on a predictable cadence, e.g. monthly) holds a realistic data sample for structured QA sign-off; and a full-copy Staging sandbox, refreshed from production shortly before each release, is where final pre-production validation and performance/UAT testing against production-like data and volume happens. Release cadence should be a fixed, predictable rhythm (e.g. a two-week sprint cadence with releases every sprint or every other sprint) rather than ad hoc 'whenever it's ready,' because a predictable cadence lets QA, UAT, and business stakeholders plan their own validation windows around it instead of constant fire-drill releases. The current single-shared-sandbox collision problem is specifically solved by giving each developer their own isolated environment for actual development work, reserving the shared environments purely for integration and validation stages where multiple people's work genuinely needs to coexist.
questions.professionalAnswer: The core problem right now is that one shared sandbox is being asked to do two completely different jobs at once -- individual development and integration validation -- and that's exactly what's causing collisions. I'd give every developer their own isolated environment, ideally scratch orgs, for actual day-to-day feature work, so nobody's stepping on anyone else's half-finished changes or stale data. Above that, I'd want one shared integration sandbox where merged feature branches come together and get tested as a whole before QA even sees it, then a separate QA/UAT sandbox refreshed on a predictable schedule with realistic data, and a full-copy staging sandbox refreshed right before each release for final validation against real production-scale data. On cadence, I'd push for something fixed and predictable -- every sprint or every other sprint -- rather than releasing whenever something feels ready, because a known rhythm is what actually lets QA and business stakeholders plan their validation time instead of scrambling every time engineering declares something's done.
commonMistakes: Proposing more sandboxes without separating them by actual purpose (dev vs. integration vs. QA vs. staging)
Not addressing that individual developers need isolated environments to stop collisions at the source
Leaving release cadence ad hoc instead of proposing a fixed, predictable rhythm
Not including a full-copy staging environment refreshed close to release for realistic final validation
keyPoints: Individual developers need isolated environments (scratch orgs or Developer sandboxes) to eliminate collisions
Shared environments should be reserved for integration, QA/UAT, and staging -- not individual development
A full-copy staging sandbox refreshed near release time supports realistic pre-production validation
A fixed, predictable release cadence lets stakeholders plan validation windows instead of reacting to fire drills

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly separates sandbox types by actual purpose
Correctly solves the root collision problem via individual dev environments
Proposes a sound, predictable release cadence
Includes realistic staging/pre-production validation

questions.title: Using Platform Events to Decouple a Fulfillment Integration
questions.prompt: An Order Management integration currently makes a synchronous REST callout to a fulfillment system every time an Opportunity closes, and that fulfillment system's occasional slowness is now causing Opportunity close actions to feel sluggish for users. How would you redesign this using an event-driven approach?
questions.modelAnswer: The redesign publishes a custom Platform Event (for example, Order_Ready_For_Fulfillment__e) from the Opportunity close logic instead of making the synchronous callout directly, which decouples the user-facing save from the fulfillment system's response time entirely -- publishing a platform event is a fast, in-transaction operation, not a network call waiting on an external system, so the Opportunity close completes quickly regardless of how the fulfillment system is performing. A separate subscriber -- either an Apex trigger on the platform event (processing asynchronously) or an external system subscribed directly via CometD/Pub/Sub API -- picks up the event and performs the actual callout to the fulfillment system outside the user's save transaction, with its own retry and error-handling logic that doesn't block or fail the original Opportunity update if the fulfillment system is slow or briefly unavailable. This also naturally supports multiple independent subscribers if other systems eventually need to react to the same 'order ready for fulfillment' business event, without the Opportunity close logic needing to know or care how many systems care about that event.
questions.professionalAnswer: The fix here is to stop making the user's save wait on a system we don't control the performance of. Instead of calling the fulfillment system directly and synchronously when the Opportunity closes, I'd publish a Platform Event right there in the close logic -- publishing an event is fast and happens in-transaction, so the save itself completes quickly no matter how the fulfillment system is behaving that day. Something separate -- an Apex trigger on the event, or the fulfillment system subscribing directly via CometD or the Pub/Sub API -- picks that event up and does the actual callout asynchronously, with its own retry logic if the fulfillment system is slow or briefly down, completely outside the path the user is waiting on. The part I like about this approach beyond just fixing the slowness complaint is that it's genuinely decoupled now -- if a second system eventually needs to react to an order being ready for fulfillment too, it just subscribes to the same event, and the Opportunity close code never has to change or even know that happened.
commonMistakes: Just wrapping the existing synchronous callout in a @future method without actually decoupling via an event
Not addressing retry/error handling for the fulfillment callout once it's moved to the async subscriber
Missing the multi-subscriber decoupling benefit as part of the architectural justification
Proposing Change Data Capture instead of a custom Platform Event, when the trigger is a business action, not a raw field change
keyPoints: Publishing a Platform Event is fast and in-transaction, decoupling the save from the external callout entirely
A separate subscriber performs the actual callout asynchronously, with its own retry/error handling
This naturally supports multiple independent subscribers without changing the publishing logic
A custom Platform Event, not CDC, is correct here since this represents a business action, not a raw field change

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly proposes publishing a custom Platform Event to decouple the save
Correctly describes an async subscriber performing the actual callout with retry handling
Explains the multi-subscriber decoupling benefit
Correctly chooses a custom Platform Event over CDC for this business-action scenario

questions.title: Choosing Between a Batch Interface, Platform Events, and Bulk API for a Three-System Sync
questions.prompt: An ERP system, Salesforce, and a marketing automation platform all need to stay roughly in sync on Account data, but true real-time sync isn't actually required -- 'within an hour or so' is fine for the business. What integration pattern do you propose, and why not something more real-time?
questions.modelAnswer: Since the actual business requirement is near-real-time (within an hour), not true real-time, a scheduled batch synchronization pattern using the Bulk API for each direction of data flow is the right default, because it avoids the real operational cost of building and maintaining an event-driven real-time pipeline (durable subscribers, replay/retry handling, monitoring for dropped events) for a requirement that doesn't actually need that level of immediacy. Each system extracts changed records since its last successful sync run (using a LastModifiedDate-based delta or a dedicated sync-tracking field) via Bulk API, loads them into the receiving system, and a middleware/integration layer (MuleSoft, an iPaaS tool, or a simpler custom scheduled job) orchestrates the three-way reconciliation and conflict resolution rules (which system wins if the same field changed in both places since the last sync). Choosing Platform Events here for true real-time push would be over-engineering relative to the stated requirement -- it adds subscriber durability, replay-window, and monitoring complexity that provides no actual business value if an hour of staleness is genuinely acceptable, and reserving event-driven architecture for scenarios that truly need sub-minute propagation keeps the overall integration estate simpler and cheaper to operate.
questions.professionalAnswer: The detail that drives my answer here is 'an hour or so is fine' -- that's explicitly not a real-time requirement, so I wouldn't reach for Platform Events or Streaming API just because they're the more sophisticated-sounding option. A scheduled batch sync using the Bulk API in each direction, running on an interval well inside that hour tolerance, does the job with a lot less operational overhead -- no durable subscriber infrastructure to maintain, no replay-window management, no monitoring for silently dropped events, because there's nothing streaming to drop. Each leg just extracts what's changed since the last successful run using a modified-date or sync-tracking field, and some middleware layer handles reconciling the three systems and picking a winner if the same Account got touched in two places since the last sync. I'd actively push back if someone proposed event-driven real-time sync here, honestly -- it's solving a problem the business didn't actually ask for, at a real ongoing operational cost that outweighs the benefit when an hour of staleness is explicitly fine.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to Platform Events or Streaming API because they seem more 'architecturally impressive' than the requirement calls for
Not proposing a delta-extraction mechanism (LastModifiedDate or sync-tracking field) for the batch sync
Missing the need for conflict-resolution rules when three systems can all independently modify the same data
Not weighing the real operational cost difference between batch and event-driven approaches
keyPoints: The stated 'within an hour' tolerance means a scheduled batch pattern, not real-time event-driven architecture, is correct
Bulk API with a delta-extraction mechanism handles each sync direction efficiently
A middleware/orchestration layer must handle three-way conflict resolution rules
Choosing event-driven architecture here would be over-engineering relative to the actual requirement

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly matches the integration pattern to the actual latency requirement
Correctly proposes Bulk API with delta extraction for the batch sync
Addresses three-way conflict resolution
Explicitly explains why a more real-time pattern would be over-engineering here

questions.title: Designing an LDV-Aware Data Model for a New High-Volume Custom Object
questions.prompt: A new custom object, 'Usage_Event__c', is expected to generate 5 million records per month. Design the object's data model and query access pattern from day one to avoid an LDV crisis a year from now.
questions.modelAnswer: At 5 million records a month, this object will cross tens of millions of rows within its first year, so it needs to be designed for LDV from day one rather than retrofitted later. Key decisions: evaluate whether Usage_Event__c genuinely needs to be a standard custom object at all, versus a Big Object, which is purpose-built for exactly this volume and access pattern (massive record counts with simple, indexed-key-based access, no roll-up summaries or complex declarative automation needed) -- if the access pattern really is 'look up events for a given record/time range' rather than complex relational querying, Big Objects avoid the LDV problems a standard object would eventually hit. If a standard object is required (because of a genuine need for triggers, roll-up summaries, or declarative automation against it), the lookup field to its parent (likely a Master-Detail or Lookup to Account or a related transactional object) and any date field used for filtering must be planned as the primary query-access fields from the start, since those will be the fields every report and integration filters on, and they're auto-indexed by virtue of being a lookup/CreatedDate-type field. Avoid any per-record triggers or automation on this object beyond what's strictly necessary, since even bulk-safe automation adds real per-record processing cost multiplied across tens of millions of rows monthly; and establish an archiving/purge policy (moving records older than a defined window to an external warehouse via Bulk API, or simply deleting them if retention requirements allow) before the object reaches a size where that becomes an emergency project instead of a planned one.
questions.professionalAnswer: Five million rows a month means I'm designing for LDV on day one, not waiting for it to become a problem. The first real question I'd ask is whether this even needs to be a standard custom object -- if the actual access pattern is just 'give me events for this record in this time range,' a Big Object is built exactly for that scale and access shape, and sidesteps a whole category of LDV problems a standard object would eventually hit. If there's a real reason it has to be a standard object -- needing triggers or roll-ups, say -- then the fields I expect every report and integration to filter on, almost certainly a parent lookup and a date field, need to be the ones I'm planning the whole access pattern around from the start, since those are the auto-indexed fields that keep queries selective at this volume. I'd also be deliberately stingy about adding any per-record automation on this object, because even perfectly bulk-safe logic still costs something multiplied across tens of millions of rows a month. And I'd get an archiving or purge policy defined and built before the object's even live, not a year from now when it's suddenly an emergency, because by the time someone notices the problem at this volume, it's already a much bigger cleanup than if it'd been planned from day one.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to a standard custom object without evaluating whether a Big Object fits the actual access pattern better
Not identifying which fields need to be the primary, indexed query-access pattern from the start
Adding unnecessary per-record automation that multiplies cost across tens of millions of rows
Deferring archiving/purge policy design until volume becomes an actual crisis
keyPoints: Evaluate Big Objects first if the access pattern is simple, high-volume, key-based lookup
If a standard object is needed, plan the primary filterable/indexed fields (lookup, date) from day one
Minimize per-record automation given the cost multiplies across tens of millions of monthly rows
Design an archiving/purge policy before volume makes it an emergency

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly evaluates Big Objects as a real alternative to a standard custom object
Correctly identifies the primary indexed query-access fields to design around
Addresses minimizing per-record automation cost at this volume
Proposes a proactive archiving/purge policy

questions.title: CRM Analytics vs. Traditional Reports and Dashboards: The Real Recommendation Criteria
questions.prompt: A business stakeholder asks why you'd recommend CRM Analytics over just building more Salesforce reports and dashboards for a complex cross-object analysis need. What's the actual decision framework?
questions.modelAnswer: Standard Salesforce reports are built directly against live, row-level-secured org data through a report type, which caps what's practically achievable for complex cross-object blending (joined reports support a limited number of blocks and have real limitations on how many genuinely different objects can be combined meaningfully), and performance degrades as data volume and report complexity grow since every report run queries live data under full sharing enforcement. CRM Analytics pre-processes and denormalizes data into purpose-built datasets via dataflows/recipes ahead of time, which supports much richer cross-object analysis (blending many data sources, including external, non-Salesforce data), much faster interactive exploration (CRM Analytics' columnar, in-memory engine is built for exactly this), and visualizations (binned analysis, what-if exploration, predictive insights via Einstein Discovery) standard dashboards can't offer at all. The tradeoff is that CRM Analytics data is refreshed on a schedule (not always live to-the-second like a standard report), and it requires real setup investment (dataflow/recipe design, security predicate configuration to replicate row-level security CRM Analytics doesn't inherit automatically from Salesforce sharing). The right recommendation depends on the actual need: if the ask is a handful of straightforward operational reports viewed by a modest number of users, standard reports/dashboards remain the simpler, cheaper, always-live choice; CRM Analytics earns its complexity when the analysis genuinely needs rich cross-object/external blending, heavy interactive exploration, or scale that standard reporting's live-query model can't comfortably support.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't jump straight to recommending CRM Analytics just because it's the more sophisticated-sounding tool -- the real question is what the analysis actually needs that standard reports genuinely can't give. Standard reports query live Salesforce data in real time with full sharing enforcement, which is great for straightforward operational reporting, but joined reports hit real limits once you're trying to blend a lot of genuinely different objects together, and performance starts to suffer as data volume grows since every report run is a live query. CRM Analytics' whole value proposition is that it pre-processes data into a purpose-built dataset ahead of time, so exploration against it is fast and can blend sources standard reports simply can't touch, including non-Salesforce data -- but that comes with real setup cost, building dataflows or recipes, and critically, security predicates, because CRM Analytics doesn't automatically inherit Salesforce's row-level sharing the way a standard report does, so that has to be deliberately configured. If this stakeholder just needs a handful of operational reports for a modest number of users, I'd say stick with standard reports, it's simpler and always live. If the ask is genuinely rich cross-object or external-data analysis at scale, that's when CRM Analytics earns the extra setup investment.
commonMistakes: Recommending CRM Analytics by default without weighing it against the simpler standard-reports option
Not mentioning that CRM Analytics data is refreshed on a schedule, not always live
Missing that CRM Analytics requires explicit security predicate configuration to replicate row-level sharing
Not naming the real limits of joined reports that justify CRM Analytics for genuinely complex cases
keyPoints: Standard reports query live data with automatic sharing enforcement but have real limits on cross-object blending complexity
CRM Analytics pre-processes data for fast, rich cross-object and external-data analysis at the cost of being schedule-refreshed
CRM Analytics requires explicit security predicate setup since it doesn't automatically inherit Salesforce sharing
The right recommendation depends on actual analysis complexity and scale, not defaulting to the more advanced tool
