evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames the decision as need-driven, not a default preference
Correctly explains standard reports' live-data/sharing-enforcement tradeoffs
Correctly explains CRM Analytics' pre-processing model and security predicate requirement
Gives a clear, defensible recommendation framework

questions.title: Designing a Governance Layer for Salesforce Data Feeding a Snowflake-Based Warehouse
questions.prompt: Several downstream teams now consume Salesforce data through a Snowflake warehouse populated nightly via Bulk API extracts and transformed with dbt. What data governance controls does this architecture need beyond what's already enforced inside Salesforce itself?
questions.modelAnswer: The moment Salesforce data lands in Snowflake, Salesforce's own field-level security, sharing rules, and role hierarchy no longer apply at all -- those enforce access only within Salesforce itself, so the warehouse needs its own, independently-configured access control layer (Snowflake's role-based access control, down to column-level masking policies for sensitive fields like SSN or compensation data that may have been accessible to a narrow group in Salesforce but would otherwise be visible to every warehouse consumer by default). A data classification pass is needed on every extracted field to identify what's sensitive (PII, financial, regulated) before it's exposed in any downstream model, because dbt models built on top of an unclassified raw extract can unintentionally propagate sensitive fields into marts that a much broader set of BI tool users can query. Lineage and documentation (dbt's built-in documentation and exposure tracking) need to make clear which Salesforce objects/fields feed which downstream models, so a Salesforce-side schema change can be assessed for its governance impact before it silently breaks or exposes something in a downstream model. Finally, data freshness and quality monitoring (tests on row counts, null rates, and referential integrity between the nightly extract and known Salesforce record counts) are needed because once data leaves Salesforce's live, constraint-enforcing database, nothing downstream automatically catches a partial or corrupted extract the way a live Salesforce query naturally would.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'd flag immediately is that the second this data lands in Snowflake, every access control Salesforce was enforcing -- field-level security, sharing rules, role hierarchy -- just stops applying, because none of that travels with the data. So the warehouse needs its own real access control, built in Snowflake itself, down to column-level masking for anything sensitive that was narrowly restricted inside Salesforce but would otherwise be wide open to every analyst with warehouse access by default. Before any of that, I'd want a data classification pass on the extracted fields themselves -- which ones are actually PII, financial, or otherwise regulated -- because a dbt model built on an unclassified raw extract can quietly propagate a sensitive field into a mart that way more people can query than ever had access to it inside Salesforce. I'd also want real lineage and documentation, so when something changes on the Salesforce side, whoever's making that change can actually see what downstream models depend on it, instead of finding out from an angry analyst three weeks later. And I'd put actual data quality tests on the extract-to-warehouse pipeline itself -- row counts, null checks, referential checks against known Salesforce totals -- because once data's out of Salesforce's live database, nothing's automatically catching a bad or partial load the way Salesforce's own constraints would have.
commonMistakes: Assuming Salesforce's sharing/FLS controls somehow carry over into the warehouse automatically
Not proposing a data classification step before sensitive fields reach downstream dbt models
Missing lineage/documentation as a governance control, not just a nice-to-have
Not addressing data quality/freshness monitoring on the extract pipeline itself
keyPoints: Salesforce's access controls do not carry over into the warehouse; independent RBAC and masking are required
Fields need classification before they reach downstream models to prevent unintended sensitive-data propagation
Lineage and documentation let schema changes be assessed for downstream governance impact before they break something
Data quality/freshness monitoring on the pipeline replaces the implicit integrity checks a live Salesforce query provides

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies that Salesforce access controls don't transfer to the warehouse
Proposes a correct data classification/masking approach for sensitive fields
Addresses lineage/documentation as a governance need
Addresses data quality/freshness monitoring on the pipeline

questions.title: Architecting a Snowflake, dbt, and Airflow Pipeline for Enterprise Salesforce Reporting
questions.prompt: Leadership wants a single enterprise reporting layer that blends Salesforce Opportunity/Account data with data from two other internal systems, refreshed nightly, with transformations that are testable and reviewable by the team rather than living in ad hoc SQL scripts. Design the overall pipeline architecture and explain each tool's role.
questions.modelAnswer: Airflow is the orchestration layer: a DAG schedules and sequences the nightly run, triggering extraction from Salesforce (via Bulk API) and the two other internal systems into Snowflake's raw/landing schema first, then triggering the dbt run only after all extracts have completed successfully, with task dependencies making that ordering explicit rather than hoping three independent cron jobs happen to finish in time. Snowflake is the storage and compute layer, holding the raw extracted data plus every transformed layer dbt builds on top of it, and its separation of storage from compute (virtual warehouses) lets the nightly transformation workload scale independently of whatever other querying is happening against the warehouse during the day. dbt is the transformation layer, where staging models clean and type each raw source, intermediate models encode the actual business logic (how Opportunities, Accounts, and the two other systems' records relate and combine), and mart models produce the final wide, reporting-ready tables the BI tool queries -- critically, this logic lives in version-controlled, testable SQL files with dbt's built-in testing framework enforcing data-quality assumptions (uniqueness, referential integrity, non-null constraints) automatically on every run, which replaces the 'ad hoc SQL scripts nobody reviews' problem directly. Airflow re-triggers a BI tool cache refresh or simply completes once dbt's run succeeds, and failure at any stage (a failed extract, a failed dbt test) should halt the pipeline before bad or incomplete data reaches the reporting layer, rather than silently publishing a partial refresh.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe each tool's job as genuinely distinct, because that's what actually makes this maintainable instead of just three tools duct-taped together. Airflow's job is purely sequencing and scheduling -- it makes sure the Salesforce extract, the two other systems' extracts, and the dbt run happen in the right order every night, with explicit dependencies, not three separate cron jobs that happen to usually finish in time. Snowflake is just where everything lives and gets computed, raw data and every transformed layer dbt builds. dbt is where the actual thinking happens -- staging models clean up each raw source, intermediate models encode the real business logic of how these three systems' data relate to each other, and mart models are the final, wide tables the BI tool actually queries. The part that directly answers leadership's 'testable and reviewable' ask is that this logic is just SQL files in version control, with dbt's test framework checking real data-quality assumptions automatically on every run -- that's the replacement for ad hoc scripts nobody can review, because now there's an actual pull request and a test suite standing between a change and production data.
commonMistakes: Conflating the three tools' roles instead of clearly separating orchestration, storage/compute, and transformation
Not making extract-before-transform task dependencies explicit in the Airflow DAG
Missing dbt's built-in testing framework as the direct answer to the 'testable and reviewable' requirement
Not halting the pipeline on a failed extract or failed test, risking a partial or bad refresh reaching reporting
keyPoints: Airflow orchestrates and sequences; Snowflake stores and computes; dbt transforms and tests
Explicit task dependencies ensure extraction completes before transformation begins
dbt's staging/intermediate/mart layering plus its test framework directly replaces ad hoc, unreviewed SQL scripts
The pipeline should halt on failure rather than silently publishing a partial or bad refresh

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly assigns and distinguishes the role of each tool in the pipeline
Correctly designs task dependencies and sequencing in Airflow
Correctly maps dbt's layering and testing to the 'testable and reviewable' requirement
Addresses failure handling to prevent partial/bad data reaching reporting

questions.title: System Design: Choosing the Right Integration Pattern for a Real-Time Order-to-Cash Flow
questions.prompt: A retail company wants Salesforce (handling Opportunities and Orders) to drive a real-time order-to-cash flow: the moment an Order is activated, inventory needs to be checked and reserved in an external warehouse management system, a confirmation needs to reach the customer within seconds, and a separate finance system needs the invoice data, but finance's own batch processing only runs twice daily. Design the full integration architecture, justifying the specific API/pattern choice for each leg of this flow.
questions.modelAnswer: This flow needs three different integration patterns, not one: a synchronous REST callout for inventory check-and-reserve, since Order activation's own success genuinely depends on an immediate answer; an async Platform Event plus a lightweight subscriber for the customer confirmation, since 'within seconds' doesn't require blocking the Order transaction itself; and a scheduled Bulk API extract for finance invoice data, matched to finance's actual twice-daily cadence rather than over-built as real-time. See the deep-dive walkthrough for the full reasoning and design detail behind each leg, and why they must fail independently of each other.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back immediately on treating this as one integration problem -- it's genuinely three different requirements wearing one request. I'd walk through each leg exactly as laid out in the deep dive: synchronous REST for inventory because the order activation's outcome actually depends on that answer right then, an async platform event plus a subscriber for the customer confirmation since fast doesn't mean blocking, and a scheduled Bulk API extract for finance matched to their real twice-daily cadence instead of building real-time plumbing nobody asked for. See the deep-dive sections for the full justification on each leg and how I'd make sure a failure in one never takes down the others.
commonMistakes: Designing one integration pattern for the whole flow instead of recognizing three distinct requirements
Making the customer confirmation synchronous and blocking Order activation on notification service latency
Over-building a real-time integration for finance when their actual processing cadence is twice daily
Not designing for independent failure isolation across the three legs
Missing a clear failure/rollback path for the inventory leg if the warehouse system doesn't confirm reservation
keyPoints: Decomposes the single request into three legs with genuinely different latency/consistency needs
Correctly uses a synchronous REST callout only where the business outcome truly depends on an immediate answer
Uses an async Platform Event plus subscriber for the customer confirmation instead of blocking the main transaction
Matches the finance integration's cadence to finance's actual twice-daily processing, avoiding over-engineering
Designs for independent failure isolation and leg-specific monitoring/alerting

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly decomposes the flow into three distinct integration requirements
Correctly justifies the synchronous REST pattern for the inventory leg specifically
Correctly justifies the async event-driven pattern for the confirmation leg
Correctly matches the finance leg's pattern to its actual batch cadence
Addresses failure isolation and monitoring across all three legs

deepDive.heading: Decompose the single request into three genuinely different integration requirements
deepDive.content: Treating this as one integration problem is the first mistake to avoid. There are three distinct legs with different latency, volume, and consistency needs: (1) inventory check-and-reserve, which needs a synchronous, immediate answer because the Order activation flow's success depends on knowing right then whether inventory is actually available; (2) customer confirmation, which needs to happen within seconds but doesn't need to block the Order activation transaction itself; (3) finance invoice data, which explicitly tolerates batch timing since finance only processes twice daily. Each leg gets its own pattern, chosen for its own requirement, not one pattern forced across all three.

deepDive.heading: Leg 1 — Inventory check-and-reserve: synchronous REST callout
deepDive.content: Because the Order activation's own success depends on knowing immediately whether inventory can be reserved, this has to be a synchronous REST callout from Apex to the warehouse management system's reservation API, made from within the Order activation transaction (via a Queueable if the activation itself is already async, or a direct callout if the activation flow allows synchronous callouts). The callout should have a short, explicit timeout and a clear failure path -- if the warehouse system doesn't confirm reservation, the Order activation itself should fail or roll back to a 'pending inventory' state rather than silently proceeding as if reservation succeeded. Named Credentials handle the authentication and endpoint configuration so the Apex code has zero hardcoded secrets or URLs. This leg is the one place in the whole flow where synchronous, blocking behavior is actually correct, precisely because the business outcome (can we promise this order?) genuinely depends on the answer before proceeding.

deepDive.heading: Leg 2 — Customer confirmation: async Platform Event triggering a notification service
deepDive.content: A 'within seconds' requirement does not mean synchronous -- it means fast, but it does not need to block the Order activation transaction, and forcing it to be synchronous would mean the customer-facing confirmation's reliability is now coupled to the Order save completing instantly. The better design publishes a custom Platform Event (Order_Activated__e) as part of the Order activation transaction -- a fast, in-transaction operation -- and a separate async subscriber (a Queueable triggered by the platform event, or an external notification service subscribed via CometD/Pub/Sub API) sends the actual customer confirmation (email, SMS, push). This keeps the Order activation fast and decoupled from the notification channel's own latency or occasional slowness, while still comfortably meeting a 'within seconds' real-world expectation, since platform event delivery and a lightweight subscriber action both happen on the order of seconds, not minutes.

deepDive.heading: Leg 3 — Finance invoice data: scheduled Bulk API batch extract, not an API matched to finance's actual cadence
deepDive.content: Since finance explicitly only processes twice daily, building a real-time integration leg for this would be pure over-engineering -- there is no business value in delivering invoice data in real time to a system that won't look at it until its next scheduled batch run anyway. The correct design is a scheduled Bulk API extract (or a simpler scheduled Apex/middleware job for lower volume) that runs shortly before each of finance's two daily processing windows, pulling newly-activated Orders' invoice data since the last successful extract. This leg should use a delta-extraction pattern (a LastModifiedDate filter or a dedicated sync-tracking field) rather than full extracts each time, and should log extract success/failure distinctly from the other two legs, since a failure here has a very different urgency profile (next batch window, not seconds) than a failure in the inventory or confirmation legs.

deepDive.heading: Tie it together: failure isolation and monitoring across all three legs
deepDive.content: The critical system-design insight is that these three legs must fail independently -- a slow or failing finance extract must never block or delay Order activation or inventory reservation, and a notification service outage must never prevent an Order from being confirmed as inventory-reserved even if the customer doesn't get an email right away. This is why only the inventory leg is synchronous within the Order activation transaction; the other two are deliberately decoupled via an event and a schedule, respectively. Monitoring needs to be leg-specific too: an inventory callout failure needs immediate, visible alerting since it affects whether an order can actually be fulfilled; a notification delivery failure needs a retry queue and delayed alerting, not an urgent page; and a finance extract failure needs to be caught and resolved before the next twice-daily processing window, which is a very different SLA than the other two.

questions.title: Defending a Design Choice to a Senior Developer Who Disagrees
questions.prompt: You designed a solution using a Queueable job chain for a multi-step approval process. A senior developer on the team argues it should have been a single large Batch Apex job instead, and says so in front of the rest of the team during a design review. How do you handle it?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer treats this as a legitimate technical disagreement to resolve with reasoning in the room, not a status contest to win. The candidate should first genuinely engage with the Batch Apex suggestion rather than becoming defensive -- asking what specifically the senior developer sees as the advantage, since there may be a real consideration (data volume, a specific limit concern) worth incorporating even if the original design stands. The response should then walk through the concrete reasons Queueable chaining was chosen for this specific scenario -- likely that each approval step depends on the previous step's outcome and needs to run with its own fresh governor-limit context immediately after the prior step rather than waiting for a scheduled batch window, which Batch Apex's start/execute/finish structure doesn't naturally express for a sequential, conditional, low-volume workflow. If the senior developer's concern turns out valid (for example, if volume is actually higher than the design accounted for), a good answer updates the design; if not, the candidate holds the position with calm, specific technical reasoning rather than either capitulating to seniority or escalating into a visible conflict in front of the team.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't get defensive about it in the room, even though it's a little uncomfortable being challenged in front of the team -- I'd actually ask him what he's seeing that makes Batch feel like the better fit, because there's a real chance he's flagging something legitimate I didn't fully weigh, like a volume assumption. Assuming he's thinking of raw throughput and I know this is a sequential approval chain where each step depends on the outcome of the one before it, I'd walk through that specifically -- Batch's start/execute/finish shape is built for processing a big, mostly-independent chunk of records, not a dependent, step-by-step workflow where each stage needs to react to what just happened. If it turns out he's right about something I missed, I'll say so and adjust the design right there -- that's not a loss, that's the design review doing its job. But if I'm confident in the reasoning, I'll hold the position calmly with the specific technical reason, not by pulling rank or getting defensive, because the goal of that room is the best design, not who wins the argument.
commonMistakes: Becoming defensive or dismissive instead of genuinely engaging with the alternative suggestion
Capitulating to seniority without actually evaluating whether the concern is technically valid
Escalating into a visible conflict in the design review instead of resolving it with reasoning
Not updating the design when the other person's concern turns out to be legitimate
keyPoints: Engages genuinely with the alternative suggestion rather than becoming defensive
Articulates the specific technical reasoning behind the original design choice
Updates the design if the challenge surfaces a legitimate gap, rather than defending ego
Holds the position with calm, specific reasoning if the original design is actually correct

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Engages genuinely and non-defensively with the disagreement
Articulates correct, specific technical reasoning for the design choice
Shows willingness to update the design if genuinely warranted
Maintains professional composure in a public disagreement setting

questions.title: Owning a Failed Production Deployment
questions.prompt: A deployment you approved and pushed to production Friday afternoon broke the lead conversion flow for two hours before anyone noticed, because a validation rule interaction wasn't caught in UAT. Walk through how you handle the immediate aftermath and the following week.
questions.modelAnswer: The immediate priority is containment and communication, not assigning blame: confirm the scope of impact (how many leads were affected, whether any data was lost or needs correction), roll back or hotfix the validation rule interaction as fast as safely possible, and communicate transparently and promptly to stakeholders about what broke, its impact, and the fix timeline, rather than downplaying or delaying the disclosure. In the following week, a good answer owns the decision to deploy on a Friday afternoon as part of the retrospective, without being self-flagellating about it -- a root cause analysis should identify specifically why UAT didn't catch the validation rule interaction (a gap in test coverage, a scenario nobody thought to test) and translate that into a concrete process change, such as adding that interaction pattern to a UAT checklist or reconsidering Friday-afternoon deployment timing for anything touching core flows. The response should model accountability without the defensiveness or deflection that would make the team less likely to surface the next near-miss honestly.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first two hours are about fixing it and being straight with people, not figuring out who's at fault -- I'd nail down exactly how many leads were affected and whether anything needs manual correction, get the validation rule interaction rolled back or hotfixed as fast as I safely can, and tell stakeholders plainly what broke and when it'll be fixed, instead of quietly patching it and hoping nobody noticed the two-hour window. The following week, I'm not going to pretend the Friday-afternoon timing wasn't part of the problem -- I'd own that as part of the retro, without turning it into a self-flagellation session, and focus the actual root cause analysis on why UAT specifically missed this interaction, because 'we should test more' isn't an answer, 'we should add this specific interaction pattern to the UAT checklist' is. I'd also want the team to see me own this cleanly, because if I get defensive or start finding ways to spread the blame around, that's exactly what teaches everyone to hide their own near-misses instead of surfacing them.
commonMistakes: Prioritizing blame assignment over immediate containment and stakeholder communication
Downplaying or delaying disclosure of the impact to stakeholders
Treating the retrospective as generic ('be more careful') instead of identifying a specific, actionable process gap
Becoming defensive in a way that discourages the team from surfacing future near-misses honestly
keyPoints: Immediate priority is containment (rollback/hotfix) and transparent stakeholder communication
Owns the Friday-afternoon deployment timing decision as part of the retrospective, without excessive self-blame
Root cause analysis identifies the specific UAT gap, not just 'we need to test more'
Models clean accountability to keep the team comfortable surfacing future near-misses

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly prioritizes containment and stakeholder communication immediately
Takes genuine ownership without excessive blame-deflection
Proposes a specific, actionable root-cause fix rather than a vague one
Shows awareness of how accountability modeling affects team psychological safety

questions.title: Mentoring a Junior Admin Transitioning into Development
questions.prompt: A junior admin on your team wants to move into Apex development and has started submitting pull requests with working but unbulkified, hard-to-read code. How do you mentor them without discouraging them or just rewriting everything yourself?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer avoids both extremes -- silently rewriting the code (which teaches nothing and quietly signals their work wasn't good enough to be worth explaining) and a harsh, exhaustive line-by-line teardown that would discourage someone just starting out. The right approach is a code review that asks guiding questions rather than just handing over corrected code -- for example, pointing at a SOQL query inside a loop and asking 'what happens here if this trigger fires on 200 records instead of one?' -- which lets the junior admin work through the reasoning and actually internalize the bulkification principle rather than just copying a fix. The candidate should prioritize feedback (not every stylistic nitpick matters as much as a genuine governor-limit risk) so the junior admin isn't overwhelmed with ten equally-weighted comments on their first PR, and should pair the correction with genuine credit for what the code does get right -- the logic itself being correct is real progress worth acknowledging even if the implementation needs bulkifying. Over time, pairing this with a short reading list or a specific next PR deliberately chosen to practice the pattern just corrected reinforces the lesson concretely.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just quietly rewrite their PR, even though it'd be faster -- that teaches them nothing and honestly feels a little dismissive of the effort they put in. I'd rather ask a guiding question right in the review, something like 'what happens to this query if the trigger fires on two hundred records at once instead of one?' and let them actually work through why that's a problem, because figuring it out themselves sticks a lot better than me just handing them the fixed version. I'd also make sure I'm not burying them in ten nitpicks on their first real PR -- I'd focus on the one or two things that actually matter, here, the governor-limit risk, and let smaller style stuff wait. And I'd genuinely call out what they got right, because the business logic being correct is real progress, even if the bulkification needs work -- if all they hear from me is criticism, that's the fastest way to make someone want to go back to just being an admin instead of pushing into development.
commonMistakes: Silently rewriting the code instead of using it as a teaching opportunity
Overwhelming the junior admin with every possible nitpick instead of prioritizing the most important issue
Being so gentle that the actual technical problem (unbulkified code) doesn't get clearly communicated
Not acknowledging genuine progress or correct logic, making the feedback feel purely negative
keyPoints: Uses guiding questions in code review rather than just handing over corrected code
Prioritizes the most important issue (governor-limit risk) rather than overwhelming with every nitpick
Pairs correction with genuine, specific credit for what the code does right
Reinforces the lesson concretely, e.g. through a follow-up task that practices the corrected pattern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Chooses a teaching approach (guided questions) over silent rewriting
Prioritizes feedback appropriately instead of overwhelming the junior admin
Balances correction with genuine encouragement
Proposes a concrete way to reinforce the lesson going forward

questions.title: Balancing a Tight Deadline Against Skipping Tests
questions.prompt: Two days before a committed release date, a product manager asks you to skip writing Apex tests for a new integration class and just ship with a stub test that satisfies the 75% coverage requirement, promising 'we'll add real tests next sprint.' How do you respond?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer pushes back on the specific risk a stub test creates, not just on principle: a stub test that merely satisfies the 75% coverage number without asserting real behavior gives no actual protection against the integration class breaking silently in a future deployment, which is a materially different and more dangerous situation than 'coverage is a little low.' The candidate should quantify the real tradeoff for the product manager in business terms -- what's the actual risk if this specific integration (handling real transactional or customer-facing logic) breaks silently next month with nobody noticing until a customer complains, versus the cost of a short, focused set of real tests covering the integration's critical paths rather than exhaustive edge-case coverage. A good answer looks for a middle path rather than an all-or-nothing stance: proposing real, if minimal, tests for the highest-risk paths (the success case and the most likely failure mode) that can realistically be written in the available time, rather than either capitulating entirely to the stub-test shortcut or refusing to ship on time over achieving perfect test coverage. It should also address follow-through: if 'next sprint' genuinely is the plan, get it explicitly scheduled and tracked as committed work, not a vague promise that quietly never happens.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back, but specifically on the risk, not just because 'tests are good practice' -- a stub test that only exists to hit 75% coverage doesn't actually protect anything; it just makes the number look fine while giving us zero real signal if this integration breaks the next time someone touches related code. I'd frame it for the PM in terms they'll actually weigh -- if this integration silently fails next month, what does that cost us, versus what does it cost to write real tests for just the critical paths right now, not full exhaustive coverage, just the success case and the most likely way this breaks. I'm not going to insist on perfect coverage and blow the deadline over it, but I'm also not going to ship a stub test that's really just there to trick the coverage gate. And if 'next sprint' is genuinely the plan for the rest, I want that actually on the sprint board as committed work, not a verbal promise that quietly evaporates once the pressure's off, because I've seen that exact promise not happen before.
commonMistakes: Either capitulating entirely to the stub-test shortcut or refusing any compromise and missing the deadline unnecessarily
Framing the pushback as abstract principle ('tests are important') instead of the concrete business risk
Not proposing a realistic middle-ground (minimal real tests on critical paths) within the actual time available
Accepting a vague 'next sprint' promise without getting it explicitly scheduled and tracked
keyPoints: Distinguishes a stub test (no real protection) from genuinely low coverage as a materially worse situation
Frames the risk in concrete business terms the product manager can actually weigh
Proposes a realistic middle path: minimal real tests on the highest-risk paths within the available time
Ensures any deferred work ('next sprint') is explicitly tracked, not a vague unenforced promise

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the real risk a stub test creates, not just a coverage-number concern
Frames the tradeoff in concrete business terms for the stakeholder
Proposes a realistic, scoped middle-ground solution
Addresses accountability for any genuinely deferred work

questions.title: Disagreeing with Another Architect on an Integration Approach
questions.prompt: You and a peer architect disagree on whether a new integration should use Platform Events or a simple scheduled batch sync. The conversation is becoming circular in a planning meeting with the engineering director watching. How do you move it forward productively?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer recognizes that a circular disagreement in front of leadership is usually a sign the two architects are arguing from different unstated assumptions about the actual requirement, not a sign one person is simply wrong -- so the productive move is to pause the back-and-forth and explicitly surface the requirement both positions depend on: what is the actual required latency for this integration, and is it genuinely sub-minute (favoring Platform Events) or is 'within an hour or so' acceptable (favoring a much simpler batch sync)? The candidate should propose settling the disagreement with that concrete business input rather than continuing to argue architectural preference in the abstract, ideally by asking the business stakeholder in the room (or tabling the decision briefly to go confirm) rather than each architect continuing to assert their own assumption about what the business needs. This response should also model collaborative behavior for the director watching: disagreement resolved through a concrete decision criterion, not through who argues more persistently or has more seniority.
questions.professionalAnswer: When I notice we're just going in circles, I'd stop and name it out loud -- 'I think we're actually disagreeing about what latency this integration genuinely needs, not about which technology is better in the abstract.' If the real requirement is sub-second or near-real-time, Platform Events wins that argument easily; if an hour of staleness is actually fine, a scheduled batch sync is simpler and I'd drop my preference for the fancier option without much fuss. So instead of continuing to go back and forth with the director watching, I'd ask whoever in the room actually owns that requirement, or offer to go confirm it with the business stakeholder before we commit either direction. I think that's actually the more impressive thing to demonstrate in front of leadership anyway -- not winning the argument, but showing that two senior people can de-escalate a disagreement by finding the actual deciding fact instead of just repeating positions at each other.
commonMistakes: Continuing to argue architectural preference instead of identifying the unstated requirement driving the disagreement
Trying to 'win' the disagreement in front of the director rather than resolving it with a concrete criterion
Not proposing a clear way to actually get the missing information (asking the stakeholder) rather than continuing to guess
Being unwilling to drop a technical preference once the actual requirement clearly favors the other approach
keyPoints: Recognizes the circular disagreement likely stems from differing unstated assumptions about the real requirement
Surfaces the concrete deciding fact (actual latency requirement) rather than continuing to argue preference
Proposes confirming that fact with whoever owns the requirement rather than guessing further
Models collaborative de-escalation in front of leadership rather than trying to win the argument

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the disagreement as stemming from an unstated requirement gap
Proposes surfacing a concrete deciding criterion instead of continued argument
Proposes a realistic way to resolve the missing information
Demonstrates professional, collaborative behavior appropriate in front of leadership

questions.title: Handling Mid-Sprint Scope Creep on an Integration Project
questions.prompt: Three days into a sprint building a Named Credential-based integration, the business asks to also add support for a second, unplanned external system 'since you're already in there.' Your sprint commitment is already realistic without it. How do you handle this?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer declines to silently absorb the added scope while still engaging constructively with the underlying business need, rather than either flatly refusing or quietly trying to squeeze it in and risk both deliverables. The candidate should point out, specifically, why 'since you're already in there' understates the actual cost -- a second external system almost always means a different authentication scheme, different payload structure, and its own error-handling and testing needs, not a trivial extension of work already in flight. The right move is to offer the business a clear choice: properly scope and estimate the second integration as its own backlog item for an upcoming sprint, or, if there's a genuine urgent reason it needs to happen now, have an explicit conversation about what gets deprioritized from the current sprint to make room, rather than letting the original commitment silently slip without anyone agreeing to that tradeoff. The answer should also model this decision transparently to the rest of the team, since protecting sprint commitments deliberately (rather than hoping everything fits) is exactly the kind of behavior a senior architect should be demonstrating for less experienced team members.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back on the framing right away, but constructively -- 'since you're already in there' makes it sound like free extra work, but a second external system almost always means a different auth scheme, a different payload shape, its own error handling, its own tests -- that's not a quick add-on, that's basically a second integration. I wouldn't just quietly try to cram it in and hope both things land fine, because that's how I end up delivering neither one properly. I'd offer the real choice -- we scope and estimate the second system properly as its own item for an upcoming sprint, or if there's a genuinely urgent reason it has to happen now, let's have an honest conversation about what comes out of this sprint to make room for it. And I'd have that conversation visibly, not just quietly between me and the business stakeholder, because I want the rest of the team to see that protecting a sprint commitment is a deliberate thing I do, not something that only happens if I personally remember to push back.
commonMistakes: Silently absorbing the extra scope without renegotiating the sprint commitment
Treating the addition as trivial instead of correctly identifying the real cost (new auth, payload, error handling)
Flatly refusing without offering a constructive path forward for the genuine business need
Handling the pushback privately instead of modeling sprint-protection behavior visibly for the team
keyPoints: Correctly identifies that a second external system is a materially new scope of work, not a trivial add-on
Declines to silently absorb the scope into an already-realistic sprint commitment
Offers a clear choice: properly scope for later, or explicitly trade off current sprint scope
Models deliberate sprint-commitment protection visibly for the rest of the team

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly assesses the real scope/cost of the request rather than accepting the 'small add' framing
Declines to silently absorb the added scope
Offers a clear, constructive choice to the business stakeholder
Models the decision transparently for the team

questions.title: Explaining a Governor Limit to a Frustrated Non-Technical Stakeholder
questions.prompt: A sales operations director is frustrated that 'Salesforce can't just update all 50,000 Leads at once' from a list view action and wants to know why your team can't 'just fix it.' How do you explain the real constraint without being condescending or just saying 'it's a platform limit'?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer avoids both condescension and a purely technical dodge ('it's a governor limit, that's just how Salesforce works'), instead translating the constraint into terms the stakeholder's own role already understands -- for example, comparing it to a reasonable business policy limiting how much any one request can consume of a shared resource, so one bulk action doesn't degrade performance for every other user in the org at that moment. The candidate should acknowledge the frustration as legitimate (the business need is real and understandable) while being concrete about why an immediate 50,000-record synchronous update isn't actually possible, and should pivot quickly to the real solution rather than dwelling on the limitation -- a properly-designed Batch Apex job, which can process the same 50,000 records in manageable chunks, each within safe limits, completing in the background without requiring the stakeholder to wait at their screen, usually within a reasonable time window. A good answer sets a concrete expectation (how long this will realistically take, and that it can be set up to run on a schedule going forward if this is a recurring need) rather than leaving the conversation at 'this needs engineering work' with no actual plan.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just say 'it's a governor limit' and leave it there, because that's technically true and completely unhelpful to her. I'd frame it more like this: 'Think of it like a shared resource -- if one action tried to update all fifty thousand Leads in the same couple of seconds it takes to click a button, it would eat up so much of the system's capacity that everyone else working in Salesforce at that exact moment would feel it slow down. So there's a real, deliberate ceiling on how much any single action can do at once, specifically to protect everyone else's experience.' Then I'd move straight to the actual fix, because dwelling on the limitation doesn't help her -- 'what we can build is a batch job that processes all fifty thousand in manageable chunks in the background, so you don't have to sit and watch it, and it's done within' -- and I'd give her a real number, not a vague estimate. If this is going to be a recurring need, I'd also mention we can schedule it to just run automatically, so she's not asking for this manually every time.
commonMistakes: Explaining the limit in purely technical terms without translating it to something the stakeholder's role understands
Dismissing the frustration as unreasonable instead of acknowledging the legitimate business need
Leaving the conversation at 'this is a limitation' without pivoting to the actual solution
Not giving a concrete time expectation or follow-up plan (e.g. scheduling it if recurring)
keyPoints: Translates the governor limit into a shared-resource-protection analogy the stakeholder understands
Acknowledges the business frustration as legitimate rather than dismissing it
Pivots quickly to the real solution (Batch Apex) rather than dwelling on the limitation
Sets a concrete expectation and addresses whether this should be automated going forward

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains the constraint in accessible, non-condescending terms
Acknowledges the legitimate business frustration
Correctly pivots to Batch Apex as the real solution
Sets a concrete expectation/follow-up rather than leaving it unresolved

questions.title: Owning a Bug Your Own Code Introduced in Production
questions.prompt: A trigger you wrote three weeks ago is found to be the cause of a data-quality issue affecting roughly 800 Account records, discovered by another team member during an unrelated investigation. How do you handle being the one who introduced the bug?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer owns the bug directly and promptly rather than becoming defensive about how it was found or minimizing the impact, and treats the discoverer as someone who did the team a favor by catching it, not as someone to be defensive toward. The priority order should be: confirm the actual scope and nature of the data-quality issue precisely (which 800 records, what specifically is wrong with them, whether the corruption is still actively occurring or was a one-time bug now otherwise contained), fix the underlying trigger bug so it stops happening to any new records, and then plan the data correction for the already-affected 800 records -- likely a one-time corrective batch or data fix script, ideally validated against a sample before running broadly. The candidate should communicate this plan proactively to whoever needs to know (the data owner, possibly affected business stakeholders) rather than waiting to be asked, and should treat the root-cause conversation (why didn't a test catch this three weeks ago) constructively, as something to genuinely learn from rather than purely as self-criticism to perform.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd do is genuinely thank whoever found this, not perform gratitude, actually mean it -- they caught something that was quietly going wrong for three weeks, and that's useful, not an attack on me. Then I'd move fast on scope: exactly what's wrong with those 800 Accounts, is this still actively happening right now or was it a bug that's otherwise self-contained, because that changes how urgently I move. I'd fix the trigger itself first so nothing new gets corrupted, then separately plan the correction for the 800 already-affected records, testing that fix against a handful of them before running it broadly so I'm not compounding one bug with a second one. I'd tell the data owner and anyone affected what happened and what I'm doing about it before they have to come ask me, because waiting to be asked makes it look like I'm hoping it goes unnoticed. And honestly, I'd actually want to understand why my own tests three weeks ago didn't catch this -- not to beat myself up over it, but because that's a real, specific gap in my own test coverage habits worth fixing for next time.
commonMistakes: Becoming defensive toward the person who discovered the bug instead of treating it as a genuine catch
Fixing the trigger bug but not planning a separate corrective action for the already-affected records
Waiting to be asked about impact instead of proactively communicating the plan
Treating the root-cause reflection as pure self-criticism rather than a genuine, specific learning opportunity
keyPoints: Responds to the discoverer with genuine appreciation, not defensiveness
Confirms precise scope and whether the issue is still actively occurring before acting
Separates fixing the root-cause bug from planning the data correction for already-affected records
Communicates proactively with stakeholders rather than waiting to be asked
Treats the root-cause gap as a genuine, specific learning opportunity

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Responds to the discovery non-defensively and with genuine ownership
Correctly sequences root-cause fix before/separate from data correction
Proactively communicates scope and plan to relevant stakeholders
Treats the retrospective as a genuine learning opportunity, not performative self-criticism

questions.title: Pushing Back on a Request to Hardcode a Quick Security Workaround
questions.prompt: Under deadline pressure, a project lead asks you to hardcode an API key directly into an Apex class 'just for now, we'll move it to a Named Credential after launch' so an integration can ship on time. How do you respond?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer treats this specifically as a security risk, not just a code-quality shortcut, and explains why 'temporary' hardcoded secrets are disproportionately likely to become permanent -- once a class containing the key is deployed and the integration works, the business pressure to revisit it evaporates, while the actual exposure (the key sitting in Apex source, visible to anyone with code access, potentially in version control history even after being 'moved' later) persists. The candidate should offer the actual time cost of doing it correctly honestly -- setting up a Named Credential typically takes well under an hour for a straightforward API key/basic auth scenario, which is very unlikely to be the actual blocker on the deadline, making the 'just for now' tradeoff not really a time-savings at all once that's pointed out. A good answer proposes doing it right from the start rather than either flatly refusing the deadline pressure without offering a path forward, or complying with a security shortcoming the candidate knows is genuinely risky.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back on this one specifically because it's a security issue, not just a 'we'll clean this up later' code-quality thing -- the problem with hardcoding a key 'just for now' is that once this ships and the integration works, nobody's coming back to fix it under the same deadline pressure that got it hardcoded in the first place, and meanwhile that key is sitting in Apex source where anyone with code access can see it, possibly in version control history even after it's eventually 'moved.' But honestly, the thing I'd actually lead with is that setting up a Named Credential for a straightforward API key scenario takes maybe thirty minutes -- so this isn't really buying us meaningful time against the deadline, it's trading a real security exposure for basically nothing. I wouldn't just refuse and leave him stuck, though -- I'd do it the right way right now, since it's genuinely not the time sink he thinks it is.
commonMistakes: Treating this as a minor code-quality shortcut instead of a genuine security risk
Not pointing out that 'temporary' hardcoded secrets rarely actually get revisited once shipped
Refusing the deadline pressure without offering an actual, fast path to doing it correctly
Complying with the shortcut despite recognizing the real risk, rather than pushing back constructively
keyPoints: Identifies this as a genuine security risk, not just a deferred code-quality issue
Explains why 'temporary' hardcoded secrets tend to become permanent once shipped
Points out the actual time cost of doing it correctly is minimal, undermining the premise of the tradeoff
